The meaning is that [the world] is crowded with diverse and distinct things, denoted by various categories (*padārtha*). In this regard, concerning those categories...

The category of Śiva includes Śiva himself, His powers (śaktis), and liberated souls (muktātman), together with the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) and others. In the category of the bound soul (paśu), however, there is a collection of all those who are bound, consisting of the forms of the Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala; and in the category of fetters (pāśa), there is a collection of impurity (mala), karma, Māyā, and the powers of obstruction that constitute their effects.

Regarding the category of *paśu* (the bound soul), there is the rule (*vidhi*) concerning all those bound by nature— namely, those of the forms of *vijñānakala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala*— and regarding the category of *pāśa* (the bond), namely *mala*, *karman*, *māyā*, their effects, and the powers of obstruction;

this includes the transference (*saṃkrānti*) of initiation rites (*dīkṣā-kriyā*), ablutions (*snāna*), time, praise, and the like, as well as their application (*tadyoga*) through the channels (*nāḍī*).

The subject matter concerns the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth. Śiva, however, is characterized by the temple (*prāsāda*), as will be described hereafter. Thus, since I desire to bestow grace upon these mortals who are qualified [for this], you ought to speak to me of the scripture whose specific nature, purpose, and subject matter are distinguished.
Having understood the nature of this prayer, the Blessed One said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme essence of the scripture, extracted from the Vātula Tantra like butter from curds. (1)
And just as honey is extracted from a flower, so too has this auspicious essence been extracted from the essence.

Regarding the word "atha" (now): its commencement is established immediately following the question. However, it means that after the knowledge of the Supreme Lord, that which has ensued will be explained. And that knowledge—intended for the purpose of favoring those to be favored through the desire to compose the scripture—is the work of Him [the Lord] as the author; for without an author, there could be no composition.

Because [the world] has an origin, it cannot have no creator; nor can it have another as its creator, because those [others], despite being omniscient, would lack complete knowledge of realities such as Śiva and so forth.
Therefore, the initial mention of the category of the Lord (pati-padārtha) here is established. "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) indicates the reason; for since—

Because mortals, due to the ripening of their impurities, lack the capacity even though they have studied extensive scriptures— and because they are not qualified recipients for those [scriptures] intended to be favored by his word— for that reason, he [describes] the true existence, the ultimate reality, of the scripture consisting of mantra and tantra, which is free from mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) and restatement (anuvāda).

I shall explain, both concisely and in detail, the essential meaning, the useful nature, and the correct arrangement of things exactly as they are established. Furthermore, there exists no other scripture that is superior—being both brief in words and great in meaning. Moreover, if this [work] were not superior, it would not concern the means for achieving supreme power. If this...

How can it be said that this scripture has Śrīkaṇṭha as its author when it is stated that the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is the author? Because it was extracted from the Tantra known as the *Vātula*; [the word is derived] from the root *bādhṛ*, meaning "to churn" (*vilodane*), with the suffix *ula* added by way of the rule for irregular formations (*bāhulaka*). That which is established by this form is called *vātula*; thus, "churning" (*loḍana*)— [The text continues: ...is the churning of the ocean of the scriptures of the sixty-four Tantras, the extraction of the essence, and the manifestation of the supreme truth. Therefore, it is called the *Vātula-tantra*. Furthermore, it is called *Vātula* because it agitates the mind of the disciple; it is called *Vātula* because it agitates the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the disciple; it is called *Vātula* because it agitates the bonds of the disciple; That which is renowned as the *Tantra*— the scripture of the Supreme Lord, the *Āgneya Kālottara*, which consists of all things that obstruct knowledge and the various objects to be illuminated—
is the source; therefore, by means of that very knowledge, one should understand the essential meaning, having abandoned mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like.
When that [reality] is extracted by the intellect from those very syllables (*mātrās*) which constitute the meaning of the word, what is it like?

It is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from curd, or honey from a flower. Just as clarified butter is the essence of curd, and honey is the essence of a flower, so too is [this work] the essence of the scriptures, drawn from the *Vātula*.
From the *Catuḥśatikā* itself, this very essence has been extracted as the auspicious and faultless [teaching].
(p. 3) From the debate and the consensus regarding the essence of the *Vātula*, even the relationship beginning with the words [of the text] is established.
Two examples are given to strengthen the essential nature of that which is illustrated.

This very first sūtra constitutes the introduction here, because by way of a broad perspective (*sthūlanaya*), it contains the complete meaning of the entire treatise, including both the subject matter (*ādheya*) and its purpose (*prayojana*). Now, one might object: "In that case, a single verse ought to constitute the introductory sūtra.
This is not so; for wherever there is a collection of words governed by a single action, that alone constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).
As they say:

"That which has a single purpose is a single sentence, provided it is syntactically expectant; otherwise, if it were divided, there would be two. Now, the commencement of this very scripture is intended solely to demonstrate the brevity of the mantra.
That which is the supreme seed called Sādākhya is situated within all beings.

Regarding that which is called *nāda*, a certain proponent of the *Nādākhyamantra* says: "The gross form of sound (*dhvani*), through its various locations, attains the state of manifold phonemes (*varṇa*).
As they say: "Born from space and air, the *nāda* emerging from the body reaches the mouth."
"That which, being divided among different locations, attains the state of phonemes (varṇa), is sound (śabda). Thus [it is said].

What is it? That very thing is intended here. He says: "no. It is that which is the supreme seed (*paraṃ bījam*); that which will be described hereafter, and as stated in other scriptures, is the producer of gross mantras and so forth through the sequence beginning with the point (*bindu*).
For this reason, it is the supreme seed of the intellect regarding all objects of expression for all beings, being the first [manifestation] of the power of Great Māyā (*mahāmāyā-śakti*).
And the form of transformation is that which is called *nāda*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"From *śakti* arises *nāda*, then *bindu*, then the imperishable (*akṣara*), and from that, the *mātṛkā*;
and because it is that which is to be protected, it resides within all living beings."

Furthermore, since it is impossible for preceding [sounds] to denote an object at the time of the utterance of the final sound— given that they consist of phonemes (varṇa)— there must exist some other cause residing in each individual person. And that cannot be the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, because their status as causes is established solely through their own respective effects.

Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the existence of] a cause other than the effect, and because it would follow that the conceptualization of multiplicity would be non-existent,
this establishment of *nāda* and the establishment of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), which is its cause,
have been demonstrated in detail by the venerable [author] in the *Nādakārikā*. They have been demonstrated.

And this has been stated by us in the *Vṛttidīpikā*: "Thus [it is said]. Therefore, it should be understood from that very source. Furthermore, he states that the knowledge of this *nāda* must necessarily be imparted by the teacher:
"O Mahāsena, having known that, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds (*pāśahā*). Thus [he says].
The teacher (*deśika*) or preceptor (*ācārya*) bestows [the teachings] in two ways upon those who are qualified, through the awakening to the supreme reality (*paratattva*).

The fetters (*pāśas*) are known as impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*) belonging to *māyā*. Among these, impurity (*mala*) is the primordial veiler of the bound soul (*paśu*), consisting of the lines of obscuration (*rekhātmāvāraka*), infinite in its manifestations, pervasive, and eternal; and there is also action (*karman*).
It has as its agent a stream whose nature is beginningless; it possesses two aspects consisting of various fruits, namely *dharma* and *adharma*.

Through its own effects (*svakāryarūpeṇa*), it consists of the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*. In the gross [state], it exists through common and uncommon worlds (*bhuvana*) and bodies of the world.

The self is the object of enjoyment, and the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*) is that which produces experience and follows the nature of the fetters (*pāśa*). It is the very power of Śiva that, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), is called the "fetter" for the sake of [the soul's] bondage. For the sake of the supreme goal, this has been taught in many ways. Furthermore, their destruction is precisely the cessation of the state of being an obstacle to the person (*puruṣa*). The cutting of the fetters and so forth is performed by the Teacher (*ācārya*).

(p. 5) Just as [the neutralization of] poison occurs through a mantra, so too, by means of the mantra, for someone who is situated at a great distance, there arises that which is called "resorting to Pure Knowledge" (*śuddhavidyāśritatva*). And when that [mantra], whose nature is Sound (*nāda*), is known, then the expressive mantras—which are the transformations of that [Sound]—and their designata, possess the characteristics of "reflection" (*manana*) and "protection" (*trāṇa*); they are precisely those [mantras].

Mantras must be known and applied according to their specific functions. He who knows them thus becomes the destroyer of bonds (*pāśahā*). Now, is this *nāda* perceived only by those situated on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)? To this he replies:
"Down to cowherds, women, children, and barbarians—even those who speak common vernaculars."
The beings who have gone into the water... [have been] liberated.

Gopāla and others are well known; they are called *gopāla* because they always purify the Cow, which is the form of the scripture (*śāstra*). The "women" (*aṅganā*) are the seventy million *vidyās*; the "children" (*bāla*) are the supreme lords of mantra (*paramantreśa*), such as Maṇḍalī and others; and the "barbarians" (*mleccha*) are those who, though lacking [higher] knowledge, are established in the thicket [of practice].

The lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas), who speak Prakrit and are practitioners of yoga established in the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva), as well as the divine beings (devayonis) belonging to the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), are included [herein]. Furthermore, Brahmā and the others residing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
and the five Kārudras residing in the coverings of water and so forth— characterized by water and the rest— are inhabitants of those respective worlds.

Thus, all the selves residing in the pure and impure worlds, through their cognition of the object denoted by that sound—which is not of the nature of the Supreme Self but is restricted to each individual self—do not cease; therefore, they themselves utter and sustain it. This is the meaning. Because it takes the form of an indication within the *Sra* [text], two meanings are intended (*abhiruddham*).

And this is the intended meaning: [the power] established as residing in all beings is proven through the reflection upon the object of cognition (*bodhya-parāmarśa*), which is the effect (*kārya*) present in every person. Therefore, because it is proximate, it is indeed capable of being known. Nor is it the case that "this belongs to the pure" or "of the pure [there is] the impure" on the path of the impure (*aśuddha-adhvani*).

And it should not be suspected that [the soul] does not go [to another body], because that would entail a deviation [from the rule] in the case of the Lord (Īśvara). For, as [his movement] toward the enjoyment and liberation of each person is established here through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for his effects, so too is there no contradiction with the scriptures. As they say:
"O Utkāmadeva, if the primordial nature of consciousness were eternal,
there would be no manifestation, for that [nature] is characterized by reflective awareness."

For this very reason, the category of *paśu* (the bound soul) is also shown here to be divided into many sub-classes. If this is so, one might ask: what is the distinction between the impure self and the pure? To this he says: "Having fully understood the gross and the subtle, one should perform action as desired."

It has been stated that a pure teacher, having known the consumer of the three foods (tryannāda) residing in heaven, should perform [the rites]...; by virtue of this knowledge, his mantras become perfected. An impure teacher, however, performs worldly actions only after knowing the gross [form]; this is the distinction between the pure and the impure. Some, however, [refer to] those beginning with "called Nāda" and so forth.

They explain the Tantras as being specific types of treatises (*śāstra*). However, that explanation is characterized by such statements as "that explanation is called the gross sound" (*sthūla-śabda*) and so forth. An accomplished teacher who knows the Mantras, having understood the *nāda* (sound) which is divided according to the aforementioned distinctions, [perceives] the impurity (*mala*), since it is a synonym for the fetter (*pāśa*), as well as the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) indicated by that [impurity].

The destruction of all bonds (*pāśas*) occurs; by the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause, the meaning is that [the practitioner] becomes the destroyer of [those] bonds. It will be explained later that this is not otherwise possible for one who lacks the capacity for the destruction of bonds. Now, the extraction of the expressive mantra (*vācaka-mantra*) is indeed concise, expressed through gross terminology.

The eighth seed-syllable from the letter *ya* is *ma*; with the two eyes [the letter *i*] placed after it, and having separated them by an intervening syllable, one becomes Śiva with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

By not intending to express the letters of the *mātṛkā*, [the text] refers to the eighth letter from the one called *ya*; although it is gross, because it is the cause for the extraction (*udvāraṇa*) of all letters and the cause for the comprehension of meanings such as "Śiva" and so forth,
that seed-syllable known as *ahaṅkāra* is described in the *Samānatantro* as "ending in *sa* and all-pervading."
Also in the illustrious *Trayodaśaśatika*:
"Now, in this way, among all the vowels, [the name] remains devoid of the letter 'a'.
O Indirā, that very [name] is [formed] by the four neuter vowels beginning with 'u', excluding [the others]."
"Abiding together with the twelve measures of fever, [it is] as much as...; the means for attaining *aṇimā* and so forth are thus proclaimed.
That which is not to be uttered and is free from doubt is ordained as liberation"—thus [ends the section on] the differentiated (*sakala*) and undifferentiated (*niṣkala*).
The fourteenth chapter on division.
Kārttikeya said:
O Maheśvara, out of compassion, tell me this true nature: how is he all-pervading, and how does he exist below, above, and across? || 1 ||
The Lord said:
As long as a living being remains within the body, he exists below, above, moving horizontally, and situated within; indeed, he is everywhere.
Having understood that a living being situated on the three paths... [he] would not be liberated if there were a dissolution of this very [being]. || 3 ||
Having understood this pervasion—that [the Self] exists in all bodies with three paths and three bases—he is indeed a yogin; of this there is no doubt.
So long as one does not attain the realization of the pervasive Lord, one wanders in saṃsāra;
but having known the all-pervading God, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. || 5 ||
Just as a grass-leech, having moved from one blade of grass to another,
remains suspended above without support, even so does the living being abide here.
The upper is empty, the lower is empty, and the middle is the stainless emptiness;
he who understands this triple emptiness... O Guha! (7)
And its pervasiveness has been declared by me in brief, but not in detail;
for there is nothing more pervasive than this, even among the pervasive.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter on the Lower and the Upper.
Īśvara said:
Hereafter I shall explain how the eightfold conviction arises:
namely, the blazing of fire and likewise the touching of a tree. (1)
The paralyzing of nooses, the destruction of the sins of monasteries, the transference of the equinox, and likewise the rendering seedless; || 2 ||
It destroys domestic fevers and [brings about] the destruction of...;
thus, for one who knows this according to the rule, renown arises everywhere. || 3 ||
Oṃ hrāṃ hrauṃ hraṃ oṃ namaḥ.
It should be described as being within the stream of fire, conjoined with a thousand upward thrusts;
through the application of the five-syllable mantra, the fire blazes forth—of this there is no doubt.
Oṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ oṃ namaḥ.
And by that stream, this preparatory practice is demonstrated:
when struck with five hundred blows, the tree is brought to its end.
Oṃ hvaṃ hvauṃ hvūṃ, homage!
Furthermore, through that stream of Varuṇa, he was restored once more,
so that his body became exactly as it was before.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ oṃ namaḥ.
In the ritual application, this [mantra] causes the fetters to be paralyzed;
there is no doubt that they fall with one hundred and eight upward thrusts. (7)
Oṃ raṃ hauṃ raṃ oṃ namaḥ.
This application for the purpose of awakening among all beings by one who knows that [mantra] should be diligently employed with exactly that many *udghātas*.
Oṃ hlāṃ hlauṃ hlāṃ oṃ namaḥ.
This is the Tulāpuruṣa yoga, which occurs when ten thousand breaths have been exhaled.
For the sake of purification from the downfall of abandoning [the precepts], ... has been proclaimed. || 9 ||
Oṃ hyaṃ hyauṃ hyaṃ oṃ namaḥ. This weightiness that arises at the moment of sudden growth—[to that I bow].
Furthermore, upon ascending again, lightness is perceived just as before. || 10 ||
Oṃ hyīṃ hyauṃ hyīṃ oṃ namaḥ.
This is the yoga for the neutralization of poison; by means of the Vāruṇa breath-retention (srotas), one certainly destroys poison through exactly eight hundred exhalations.
Just as there is no ignition without fire, so too there is no seedless state [of liberation] without it;
herein, a specific distinction is prescribed by means of five hundred upward breaths (udghātas).
Oṃ hrūṃ vauṃ hrūṃ phaṇnamaḥ.
When this [mantra] is employed in its continuous flow through the application of eight hundred *udghātas*, it certainly and swiftly destroys the house. (13)
Oṃ hraṃ phaṭ auṃ hrauṃ phaṭ ............ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ.
This [mantra], when joined with the Vāruṇa stream, quickly destroys fever through a practice of exactly eight hundred udghātas. || 14 ||
(10) I have explained the application of the eight conditions; having understood them each time, the best of instructors should apply them according to the rule. (15)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, concerning the eightfold condition.
Kārtikeya said:
"O Maheśvara, what is the nature of the temple (prāsāda) to be known, and what is its pervasion (vyāpti)? What is its origin (prasūti)? Please tell me."
Īśvara said:
He who does not know the temple, whose great body consists of the five mantras and which is endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, is not called an Ācārya.
If a guru performs initiation without having correctly understood the Prāsāda [mantra], he leads both his disciple and himself downward; of this there is no doubt.
The teacher, together with his disciple, shall attain union with Śiva.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kṣobhakas, lords of the yakṣas and uragas,
kinnaras, apsarases, and siddhas— all have come forth from the palace.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, then Āditya, Śakra, Skanda, and likewise Bhṛgu.
And all other hosts of planets who dwell within the palace,
as well as these and many other sages of rigid vows— || 7 ||
They meditate upon that which is called the Supreme Haṃsa by name;
and I shall explain its division, knowing which one attains immortality.
One should know that [the face] immediately joined with the eight digits (kalās) arises from the syllable A;
the Vāma [face] is born from the syllable U, while the Aghora [face] is born from the syllable Ma. (9)
The person born from the seed-syllable (bindu) is to be known as Īśāna, who is born from the crest (śikhā);
thus, these five are remembered as originating from the temple (prāsāda).
By means of this very pleasing palace, the hundreds of thousands of millions of mantras of immeasurable power will undoubtedly become effective.
The Maruts, Anala, Śakra, and others who have been proclaimed—
born from the lotus of the palace, they all possess unfailing power.
The Earth is to be known as Sadyojāta, while Water is proclaimed as Vāmadeva; Fire is said to be Aghora, and Air is remembered as Tatpuruṣa. || 13 ||
Ākāśa, however, is Īśa, while Svayambhū is Maheśvara; Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda. || 14 ||
The Aghora is the Sāmaveda, while Puruṣa is said to be the Atharvaveda;
that which is the fifth, supreme, and subtle is Sadāśiva, the all-pervading space. || 15 ||
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā; Vāmadeva is proclaimed as Viṣṇu; Aghora has Rudra as his presiding deity; and Puruṣa is likewise Īśvara. || 16 ||
Īśāna is proclaimed as having Śiva as his presiding deity; these are declared to be the higher deities.
But that which is the sixth, supreme reality, abides in qualities beyond comparison.
His body should not be described as being composed of the qualities arising from material nature (prakṛti),
for he has realized the supreme ladder that leads to the fivefold state.
By him whose inner self was struck with wonder, knowledge was known all at once; at that very moment he spoke thus: "What is this knowledge? For it is indeed beneficial. (19)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the knowledge of the Prāsāda mantra, in the glorious Viṃśatikālottara Mahātantra.
Having bowed to Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, I compose this commentary on the two hundred [verses] of the venerable Kālottara, which brings benefit to the followers of Śiva.

For the pleasure of the learned, this concise [work] is composed by me, wherein the expansions and contractions of meter, as well as the *sphurita* and other such meters, are presented for those who are weary of prolixity.

For here, the relationship of the Śaiva scriptures as received from the Guru is twofold: common and uncommon. That characterized by the sequence of the Great Current (mahaugha-krama), found in all the Saṃhitās and consisting of Ananta and others, is common to all. However, the lineage of Gurus specific to each individual Saṃhitā is uncommon.

Kārttikeya, whose form begins with the *praṇava*, having obtained authority from his preceptor through knowledge pertaining to both [the teacher and the taught], and having understood the capacity of human beings for this great tantra by means of the reasons to be mentioned— such as their lifespan and so forth— thereupon [approached] his own guru, the Blessed One, for the sake of the good transmission.
The disciple of Kārttikeya, who was himself the grand-disciple of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, spoke thus to his own disciples; and as to what he said, he declares:
"These mortals have a lifespan of only a single kalpa, and their strength and prowess are meager."
But those who are small-minded, possessing little wealth, and filled with greed and delusion—|| 11 ||
O Lord of Gods, O Master, for the sake of favoring me, you ought to speak that which is concise in words yet great in meaning, and filled with many explanations of the subject matter.

For, in order to demonstrate that in this extensive scripture and in the performance of its meaning, only the Rudras— the gods— possess the authority of office and not humans in general, he now qualifies them.

In this world, human beings are possessed by a mental impurity consisting of greed, the craving for conditioned phenomena, and delusion—manifesting as the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self within that which is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self.
Among them, those who, through the ripening of their impurities, somehow become qualified [for practice]... (p. 13)
[The requirements] are fulfilled. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"He, whose impurities are forever destroyed, becomes dispassionate toward saṃsāra."

Because his lifespan is short, he is not at all capable of performing even the study and recitation of hundreds of mantras, such as those beginning with "vyomavyāpin," within the extensive tantras; however, he is indeed capable of practicing their meaning within a very concise [version].
As they say:
"One who is desirous, capable, and learned [is qualified], provided it has not been excluded by the scripture."

In this context, *vīrya* (diligence) is skillfulness of action, prowess, and physical agility; or rather, it is strength, valor, and enthusiasm. Furthermore, these beings of little merit and little wealth—due to their meager virtue and because all their defects such as passion have been fully manifested by that very lack of endurance—are [submerged] in the darkness of that [suffering].

One is unable to undertake the observance of vows. Due to having little wealth, they are not capable of performing extensive rites such as worship and fire-offerings (homa), which require numerous materials like camphor and sandalwood. Therefore, O Lord of Gods, O God who rules over the gods, the great ones such as the Piśācas and others, and those of divine origin—

"O Lord, for the sake of the grace of Your playful manifestation (*prabhāvanā-līlā*), and for the sake of knowledge regarding the practice of the means to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), You should explain that concise treatise which consists of mantra and tantra, in which [these topics are contained], free from explanatory or repetitive passages (*arthavāda-anuvāda*). This is the prayer.
The meaning is that it is endowed with mantras such as *parala* and others, which are few in syllables and innumerable. To show that it is not thus of little purpose, he says:

"And it is of great significance," because the great purpose—characterized by the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*)—is achieved precisely through what has been stated.

It is endowed with a purpose; thus, it is also rightly said to be joined with the subject matter (*abhidheya*), namely, with the categories of reality (*padārtha*) which are the means for [liberating] each individual soul from its bonds, or the means for enjoyment and liberation, or the ritual procedures, actions, and times appropriate [for them], designated as "Śiva," and so forth. [The text continues: "with many..."

The characteristics of the proponent (*vādin*) should also be known. In that regard, "scratching" (*ullekhana*) refers to the drawing of four lines with *darbha* grass and the like over the already completed sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the sake of purification;
one should perform this by sprinkling it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and so forth, and then with the *astra* and *kavaca* [mantras], but not otherwise.

Some explain that the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa*, are appropriate for the *atanapāta* [the scattering of the bones]; however, since only *ullekhana* (scratching) and *abhyukṣaṇa* (sprinkling) are explicitly prescribed in the scripture (*śruti*) regarding them, only those two should be performed. But surely, even if it has been consecrated by two rites, it remains unconsecrated, because the purpose of these rites is visible (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). Of those whose purpose is visible...
It is appropriate to say of things such as washing, "this has been accomplished" or "this has not," but not of those whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Consequently, even those [unseen results] must be understood as being accomplished by both [the primary and the subsidiary acts]. For it is in this way that a distinction in the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is logically established. As they say:
Due to the distinction between rituals and so forth, a distinction in the tantras is traditionally taught;
therefore, the tantra should be practiced in exactly that manner.
Or even he who, disregarding one who is well-established, acts according to another system,
having treated that sage as an authority no longer, he too is joined with unrighteousness.

Furthermore, beginning with the question "But why [are they] short-lived," etc., the Blessed One commenced to speak in brief; however, since this contradicts the initial premise regarding those who lack the qualification for the forms of mantras in the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*, if that were so, [the sequence of] bathing and so forth...

Those [details] must also indeed be performed; for it has been stated that their capacity as a cause of purification is established by the nature of the verbal injunction itself. Whatever is obtainable through the power of the words—whether it is capable of being stated, or can be spoken, or is already attained—that should be accepted from another *saṃhitā*. Thus, in a consecrated *kuṇḍa*...
As for what one should do, he says: (p.
16) "Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should perform the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa) with the heart-mantra."

The term "mantrī" (the mantra-practitioner) refers to the preceptor or other empowered authority who should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Vāgīśvarī and others, as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*),

and the eightfold placement and worship that constitute its remainder, using the *hṛdaya* mantra. Some, however, state that based on the word [in the source], the worship of Vāgīśvara must also be performed.
One should cast the *jātavedas* (fire) into the womb with the heart-mantra; then,
having performed the general purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth according to the requirements of the purpose,

one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*), and [the fire] which has been infused with the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*) or obtained through the *añjali* gesture, takes on the form of Vāgīśvara.
One should offer oblations to the Supreme Lord Śiva together with his limbs (aṅgas), which bestows all accomplishments;
then, one should worship the Blessed One along with his limbs upon the seat there, as previously described.

It shows that regarding the number of oblations (*homa-saṃkhyā*), because speech (*giraḥ*) is the primary element, one may offer with clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, or with barley (*yava*), or even with "despised" sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), provided they are not repulsive—this being said in consideration of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "One should offer ten parts," because this is for the purpose of completing the rite of oblation.

The *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) is established for the sake of accomplishing the goal, as he will state later in the section on initiation: "O Six-faced One, one should subsequently offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *Prāsāda* mantra. It is also stated in the *Samānatantra*:
"The offering of the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *dhāraṇa* (maintenance/retention) must be performed."
One should mentally recollect that which is the supreme nectar, the Sāman, as it flows forth.
In the section concerning initiation, that [method] should be applied everywhere and at all times.
"And in the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*, as well as in the rites of constant purification.

Thus [it is said]. And he should perform this rule for the fire-sacrifice (*homayajavidhi*). "In a well-kindled fire" (refers to the fire). Since the section on the mandala will be explained later, it should be performed in a fire of increased brilliance.

(p. 17) Then, because it has been stated that "one should perform [the rite] as previously described," one should perform all the services, such as water for sipping (*ācamana*) and betel (*tāmbūla*), and then perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) of Śiva together with the fire. Having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) according to the sequence taught in another *Saṃhitā*, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and the ritual of making oneself complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having presented the act of fire-oblation (*homakarma*) to Śiva who has been fully worshipped, one should perform his final dismissal (*vivisarjana*).
Thus, the rite is accomplished.
This concludes the third chapter, on the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), in the *Śrīmatkālottaravṛtti* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.

Thus, the daily obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) to be performed by those who have been initiated at subsequent times has been described. Now, he describes the mandala, which is an ancillary part of mantra-practice for any practitioner— whether a beginner or otherwise— among those engaged in the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) for the attainment of the state of being initiated:
Henceforth, I shall explain the mandala that fulfills all desires;
for in this context, the sacrifice of the mandala, the sacrificial pavilion, and the sequence of the initiatory rite (samayadīkṣā) cannot be established without [this preliminary].

Furthermore, because it will be stated that "whatever else is not mentioned, all of that should rely upon the root mantra," [the procedure is as follows]: having first prepared the sacrificial pavilion— beginning with the ritual acquisition of the ground (*bhūparigraha*) and so forth— as described in other *saṃhitās*, the preceptor, having performed his daily obligatory rites such as bathing, and having worshipped the gateway and so forth, enters the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) which has been duly prepared for the body...
Having prepared the specific sequence beginning with purification, including the *śivatanu* and *śivahasta* rites,

and having taken up the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), one should contemplate "I am Śiva. Then, having consecrated the *vikāra* and other materials, and having first performed the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should purify the pavilion and scatter the ritual offerings (*vikirān*) with the *astra-mantra*.

Having performed the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*) and other rites, having worshipped Śiva in the mandala starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), and having offered oblations to Śiva residing in the fire, one should present the *caru* as a sign of His close presence (*susānnidhya*), offer the internal sacrificial fee (*antarbali*), and [account for] the ill omens of place and time... (p. 18)

Having eaten for the purpose of producing the *nimitta*, and having worshipped Śiva for the sake of admitting the disciples, those who have received permission are led into the outer mandala; having been purified by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth,
their eyes covered with a fine cloth, they are made to enter and stand facing north in the southern direction of the deity.

Having withdrawn the consciousness from his heart into its own seed-syllable, having purified that body, and having given the hand of Śiva— consecrated as Śiva— to him, one should place a flower in his joined palms,

raise him up, remove the blindfold from his eyes, and after making him cast the flower [to determine his deity], having led him around clockwise and made him prostrate, one should lead him to the vicinity of the poor and the fire.

Having first performed the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) and offered the *sampāta* oblations numbering one hundred or more, one should then worship the Fire and Vāgīśī. Having grasped the consciousness of the disciple according to the procedure taught in another *Saṃhitā*,
and having established it within oneself, one should unite it with Vāgīśvarī for the sake of [attaining] perfection, beginning with the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*).

For the perfection of the ritual acts (*saṃskāra*), one should worship Śiva together with his limbs (*sāṅga*) using the root mantra, and having offered oblations amounting to a thousandth part of the initiation and a tenth part [of that], one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, for those observing the vows, one should offer the ancillaries of the vow (*vratāṅga*) according to another *Saṃhitā*. Thereafter, desiring to perform the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), [one should proceed] with the root mantra and so forth.

Having satiated the mantras and taken hold of the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra), O God, one should perceive therein the consciousness of the bound soul (paśu) as described in other scriptures; then, having placed upon it the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā— whether as a pregnant womb or otherwise—
one should satisfy, inflame, and restrain them, and finally lower the cord of bonds into a casket made of earthenware or similar materials.

Having prepared [the materials] and offered them to Śiva residing in the *kumbha*, and having given the *pañcagavya*, the *caru*, and the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to the disciples according to the rules, and having established [them] properly; then, having removed the defect indicated by the tooth-stick, and having restrained Śiva who resides in the fire, [one proceeds to] that place of the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth.

Having placed [the deity] in the *kalaśa* and offered the external *bali*, one should oneself consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, and then install [the deity] according to the rule. Thereafter, one should draw the mandala... having fixed [the thread] upon a pillar or a pregnant woman, having gratified, kindled, and restrained it, one should lower the cord of the noose (*pāśasūtra*) into a casket of arrows and so forth, and thus complete it.

Therefore, after the obligatory daily rites (*nityakarman*), I shall explain another [practice], the circle of limbs for occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) sacrifices, which serves the purpose of fulfilling all desires. Now, he says that:
having made it well-measured with a cord, square on all sides.
Having established the noble lotus, one should draw the maṇṭhapatra.
The pericarp (karṇika) should be one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits;
for it will be stated below that "the western door should be placed here," which implies the existence of two [doors].
For that purpose, the measurement of the maṇḍala should be understood from the *Samānatantra* as being two hundred and fifty [finger-breadths] (*sārdha-dviśatika*). As it is stated there:
"It should be ten, twelve, or sixteen cubits (*hasta*) in size."
Then, having measured it properly— neither too small nor too large— using a cord according to the procedure taught by Śrīmat Mayā and others, for a square measuring ten, twelve, or sixteen cubits,
one should [mark] within that space, in due order, an area of one cubit or...

The lotus together with its pedestal should be fashioned exactly as described in other treatises. Outside, in the four directions, four doors equal in size to the lotus should be constructed. As it is heard:
"The temple should be the measure of the lotus, and its projection should be half of that."

And in the remaining space between [the lines], the ritual procedure should be performed in the sacred field (*śiṣṭakṣetra*). Here, the pedestal, the arrangement of the threads and so forth, as well as all specific details such as the placement (*vinyāsa*), are to be understood from the *Saṃhitā* itself. Furthermore, in this case, there is only a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*), just as in the daily worship (*nityārcā*).

Showing that worship must be performed for the sake of accomplishing the common fruit of all obscurations, he restates the previously mentioned point: "But this [practice], which removes a single obscuration, is the means for accomplishing all ritual actions."

The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of emphasis (*amārthe*). Here, on the second day as well, having performed the obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), one should enter the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) and perform the ritual beginning with the binding of the previous body and ending with the worship of Gaṇapati; then, having worshipped the Lord in the mandala along with the retinue of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅgāvaraṇa*), one should perform the rites up to the offering of the recitation (*japanivedana*).

And then, because of the [instruction] "from there... [tataśca], the previously mentioned *sūtra* regarding the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the Heart in the southeast (*āgneyī*) is connected with this [text] as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). As they say:
"Whatever has a semantic connection with something, that [connection] belongs to it even if it is situated far away. How so?

Furthermore, in this very context, there is no contradiction because, according to the maxim "the aphorisms are like the meters," it serves to bring about the attainment of the desired goal. And here:
"One who desires success, being composed, should cause the western door to be carried [open]."

The final [measurement] should also be understood to apply to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). And because of this specific injunction, the *maṇḍala* has four gates... Now, in this context, he states the dimensions and shape of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the daily and occasional rites:
"One should cause a pit to be made in the southeast, measuring one cubit on all sides."
The meaning is that it should be four-cornered and one cubit on all sides. Furthermore, one should perform the ritual procedure for sacrifice in a well-kindled fire;

in all rites, such as the daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) and others, "well-kindled" is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*). [It applies] to those fires that are smokeless and well-established, for which there is beauty.
When the fire possesses fragrance, a pleasant sound, and is oily and clockwise-rotating,
one should perform the rites of sacrifice— including the mantras, libations, and offerings up to the *bali*— and bring about peace,
provided that such conditions are possible.
It has been stated that the performance of the *ekāvaraṇa-yajña* (the sacrifice of a single enclosure) should be carried out; this is now shown in detail:

"One should place the Heart-mantra in the southeast (*āgneyī*), and the Head-mantra in the southwest (*śāvī*). One should place the Śiva-mantra and the Knowledge-mantra (*vidyā*) in the southwest (*nairṛtī*), and the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*) in the northwest (*vāyavī*)."
Having placed the weapon-mantra in the directions, or Sadāśiva in the pericarp.

Having meditated upon the God in His complete form and worshipped Him, one should worship the Weapon (astra) in the petals of the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Yakṣa, and Marut; the remainder is that [the Weapon] should be placed above Śiva and Vidyā. Thus, having worshipped Śiva along with His enclosures (sāvaraṇa), the fire-rite (agnikārya) is to be performed; so it has been stated.
Let them give...
[the rest]. In brief, the ritual procedure for the *skanda* has been proclaimed by me;
omitting the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and restatements (*anuvāda*), the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) and the momentary injunctions have been stated, but not the [adhikāra]...
Therefore, one should abandon that [notion of] "it must be done" (kartavyatā) regarding latent impressions (vāsanā); for this very reason, he says:
"Whatever may be unmentioned, all that should take recourse in the Root (mūla).
Since this world is a transformation (vikṛti), whatever is unmentioned is not to be expected from the eternal Primordial Nature (prakṛti). Nor is even the unmentioned to be sought elsewhere.
From the root [text] *pā*... as it is stated in that very same place:
"The twelve vowels, excluding the neuter ones, are declared to be the *mātrās*;
the *sūtras* become like [the *mātrās*]," according to this logic, the word *mātrā* is used here in the masculine gender.
Then, having separated the twelve measures (mātrās) associated with the syllable named "Na" (the eye of Brahmā)—
meaning, having excluded those consonants from 'A' to the final 'Anusvāra'— one should apply the remaining measures beginning with 'Ā'. In this way, the six-limbed mantra [is formed] for Gaṇeśa...

By virtue of being of a single nature, he becomes Śiva. Since Brahmā and the others are presided over as his forms (*mūrti*), and because they are included within him, the sixfold nature—which was shown here through differentiation as belonging to the self of Śiva—is now analyzed in detail. (p. 22)
One should know the first to be the Heart, while the second is traditionally remembered as the Śiras;
the third is the goddess Śikhā, and the fourth shall be the Kavaca.
One should know the fifth to be Śiva and the sixth to be the Astra, ending with the Visarga.
Therefore, the intention here is that the limbs of Śiva (śivāṅga) known as Sarvātman, Śivajvālā, Piṅgala, and Śivaśāstra—
namely the Heart and so forth— are what are to be expressed, and not the limbs of Vidyā such as Vidyeśvara and the rest. This is because,
in the phrase "the fifth of the fifth," the word "fifth" serves as an indicator for that which denotes Śiva, due to the presence of the word "tu."

Alternatively, they say that because it is intended to convey a specific distinction, the six-limbed *niṣkala* temple (*prāsāda*) which is about to be described is what has been extracted here for the daily rites (*nityakarman*). That is incorrect, because those [temples] such as the *sakala* and others,

numbering eight and so forth, will be described as the causes for supernatural powers (*siddhi*) like the power of becoming small (*aṇimā*), and therefore the daily rites and so forth must be distinct from them.

However, due to the application (*viniyoga*), there is a restriction; thus, the entry of the *bindu* here into the heart and other centers is established from that very [application]. As it is said therein:
"The *anusvāra* shall be the eye, situated above all. And of these, at the beginning and the end...
The context concerning the salutation with the *praṇava* has been stated in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*.

"Mantras preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with an ending of obeisance (*namaskāra*)—all these were made by Śiva alone; they were not made by Ananta and the others. Thus he says: "This six-limbed [system] was taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self."

The meaning is "by the Supreme Self, who is beginninglessly liberated. As it is stated in the *Mantravārttika*: "Viśambhu [is the one] who discerns the general and specific attributes of the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras; for it is observed that he is the imitator of the Mantras, since he is seen to be the knower of their meaning and the performer of their expression. Thus, the Mantras have been described in brief.
They are to be employed in all ritual actions. (p.
23) He introduces the mudrās:
"I shall proclaim this mudrā by which practitioners attain success."

In this context, the mudrās are described as the powers (*śakti*) of Hara, according to the scripture: "The mudrās are not without knowledge. Mudrā is said to be the very power of Śiva, manifested through the gestures of the hands.
I shall now explain how a single mudrā alone can gladden the multitude of mantras that have been awakened and destroy all obstacles.
I shall fully explain the performance of sacrifice according to its proper sequence.

I shall briefly describe the performance of sacrifice (*yajana*) as it is said [in the scriptures], beginning from the ritual bath (*snāna*) up to the heart-sacrifice (*hṛdayāga*), without transgressing any of the prescribed rules. The meaning is that all beings indeed reside within this [sacrifice]. For this very reason, this [sacrifice] is the fundamental archetype (*prakṛti*) here, because it is complete in all its limbs; whereas the mandala-sacrifices and others depend upon this one for their requirements.

The elements are doubled because they serve as the substratum for the external sacrifice, and because bathing is prescribed here immediately after the invocation (āvāhana). Since that [bathing] cannot exist without a *liṅga*, the characteristics of the *liṅga* and its installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth are well-known from other scriptures; thus, by the phrase "in due order" (*anupūrvaśas*), the worship of the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla-pūjā*) is implied.
The sequence beginning with purification is prescribed here. For in this context, the initiated one, having performed his necessary duties,
bathed according to the rules of purification, and being free from the [ordinary] baths of water and earth, performs the Āgneya bath appropriate for the three periods of the day,
as well as the specific meditations, cleansing (mārjana), the Amṛtamanthana hymn, libations (tarpaṇa), and worship (upasthāna), remaining free from anger and possessing a gentle countenance.

Having first performed the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) and *upavinyāsa*, and having purified his body by casting away [impurities], he established a body of power (*śakti-śarīra*). Having performed the purification of the inner sacrifice (*antaryajana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the meditation (*dhyāna*), the place,
the vessel for the *arghya* offering, and the preliminary purification of the ritual substances, as well as the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*) and the purification of the mantra, he worshipped Gaṇapati.
One should begin with the worship of the Guru. Now, regarding that commencement (p.
24): one should place the heart-lotus, which has its stalk at the throat, as well as Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth, along with Vairāgya and Aiśvarya, all originating from the heart.
One should form the array of powers (śakti-vyūha) with the filaments and the lotus with the Heart-mantra;

for, due to the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the lotus, the pericarp-lotus, the Heart," the Heart is indicated as being the actual locus, and thus it is directly presided over by Śiva and Śakti.

And its *śuddhavidyā*-lotus is proclaimed; therefore, the meaning is that one should install the lotus and so forth with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). "Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth" means Dharma, Jñāna, and the rest;
and "the beginning of those two" refers to their substratum, namely Ananta. And by the word "thus" (*evam*), [one installs] the nature of Māyā with the Heart-mantra.

One should place that [deity] whose origin (*prabhava*) is the attainment of self (*ātmalābha*) in that manner; the meaning is that one should place it with the *hṛdaya* mantra. Here, the meaning itself is followed... because the meaning is more powerful than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Therefore, having first worshipped the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) with the primordial power (*purāśakti*) by means of the *praṇava*, one should thereafter [worship] the seat, Ananta, Dharma, and so forth.

Having placed the four feet upon the cover with the Heart [mantra], one should then place [the remaining parts] upon the pericarp of the Śivāsana-lotus. Then, along with the filaments, the attendant powers (śaktis) reside there as their substratum; according to other scriptures, these are the eight powers beginning with Vāmā, starting from the east.
One should place Manonmanī in the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus.

Then, with the heart-mantra, one should fashion the three mandalas— known as Anuvyūha, Sūtra, and Saṃjña— which consist of the principles (tattvas) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and the forms of Vidyā and Śiva.

However, some say that even the *śaktimaṇḍala* is the locus for the manifestation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), and that because of the proximity of the word "and" (*ca*) here, the term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) refers to the power (*śakti*)... [etc.
...having conceived the pure seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*).
p. 25) Then the practitioner should invoke the deity with the *hṛdaya* [mantra].

Immediately thereafter, because the invocation of the partless (*niṣkala*) Śiva depends upon a substratum, one should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* there, repeating it twice... [as indicated by] the word "iti" and the statement that will be spoken later, or by one who is empowered.

Furthermore, by means of the previously mentioned mantra expressing existence (*sadbhāva*), one should invoke the unmanifest form (*avyaktā mūrti*) enclosed within the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. Then, by the force of the scriptural statement beginning with "immediately endowed with the eight *kalās*," one should bestow the eye; and because of the hearing of a common *tantra* stating, "The Lord Sadāśiva is manifest from the very beginning," [one should likewise invoke] the manifest form.
One should fashion the form of Sadāśiva, which consists of all parts, by means of the *prāsāda* [mantra]; as he will say:
"He who does not know the *prāsāda*, the great body of the five mantras, [does not attain] the fruit endowed with the eighty-three... and so forth.

One should perform the invocation (āvāhana) of this [deity] with the *prāsāda* mantra, which is the heart of Supreme Śiva. As it has been said: "The supreme worship consists of resting in the final limit of the *pluta* [protracted vowel] within the *prāsāda* mantra. Furthermore, the knower of mantras should perform the invocation, as well as the bathing and worship, using the *hṛdaya* mantra alone; the word "and" (*ca*) is used here because these acts serve as indicators for other related rites.

The ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are: invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), proximity (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), the great placement (*mahānyāsa*), the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the offering of the guest-water (*arghya*), and the offering of *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; likewise, the preliminary ritual (*parikara*) consisting of bathing and anointing with oil (*abhyaṅga*).
After the immersion, the lustration, and the consecration, one should perform worship with white garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth;

offer incense, lamps, and other items for the night vigil; present mouth-fresheners, betel, and the like; again offer incense; and provide the splendor of mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, and other such riches, as well as the presentation of the sacred thread (*pavitra*).

One should perform all rites, from the recitation of mantras up to the offering, solely with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. This very point is stated: "All that is enjoined by the ritual rules should be done with the *hṛdaya* alone."
The meaning is that all the ritual procedures (vidhi) taught in the root-tantra and in the subsidiary tantras (sutrantra), which are free from defects, are to be applied here.
It is also stated in the Samānatantro:
"Whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, all of that should be performed with the heart [of the mantra]."
Even all ritual actions that are to be accomplished through other mantras, when repeated again and again, accomplish this very same one in that manner. Regarding the "rule" (niyama):
now, is there worship of Varuṇa here or not? To this, he says:
This single enclosure, however, accomplishes the purpose of all ritual actions.

"One should place the Heart [mantra] in the southeast," and so forth; the method of worship for the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*) to be described in the section on the mandala is understood here by the force of the qualification "or the eye" (*netra-vā-karaṇa*), because such worship serves as an embellishment. As it is said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "That which is unenclosed is not worthy of beauty."
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendra* as well, it is said: "The Lord shines forth unobscured by the [five] restraints.
Now, is it not the case that the *pūjāsūtra* regarding obscuration contradicts the section on the *maṇḍala*? No;
for not every statement contradicts its specific context, nor does every statement contradict its particular mode of presentation.

It cannot be restricted. Since it has been stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is established here that the worship of the inner enclosure (*pūrvāvaraṇa-pūjā*) must be performed before the offering of the food oblation (*naivedya*) at the conclusion of the worship. Furthermore, the rule for dismissal (*apavarga-vidhi*) applies here from the context of the recitation of the *Prāsāda* mantra. And because the invocation (*āvāhana*) is not required for the purpose of worship, its completion [marks the end of the rite].

The dismissal (*visarjana*) is said to be either dependent or independent, depending on whether it is preceded by the offering of supreme suffering or the assumption of signs and so forth for the sake of notification. And this [is performed] "at will" (*kāmataḥ*); here, "will" refers to all those [rites], such as the constant and occasional propitiation of mantras.
The purpose is that it alone cures the single obscuration (*ekāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, this is common to all tantras;
it refers to all dependent tantras and other streams (*srotas*), and by them, the fruits mentioned therein are indicated.
Even among those powers (*bala*), this is common, and the meaning is that it accomplishes them as well. Therefore, him—

This very [practice] is to be performed even by those seeking fruits; moreover, it is "consented to in all knowledges," meaning it is not contradicted by any of the Siddhānta scriptures, such as the Kāmika and others. What is meant is this: although this [system] has only one covering (āvaraṇa), it does not deviate from the power of the many coverings.
Thus ends the second chapter, on Sacrifice, in the commentary on the venerable *Viṃśatikālottara* composed by the illustrious Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].

Henceforth, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (agnikārya). Following worship, for the sake of the supreme Śaiva fire-offering—that is, for the purpose of generating the fire—one must perform the ritual sequence; therein, the offering into the fire should be performed with the recitation of mantras, worship, and the corresponding oblations.
He said to him:
"Scraping with the ritual manual is known as sprinkling with the armor-mantra."
In response to the inquiry as to where this description originates:
"One should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made in the southeast, measuring one cubit on all sides."

Thus, from the section on the mandala, the statement stands [in context]. And because its other specific details are being stated, it is rightly said—along with the measurements of the girdles and so forth—that [the rite] is performed by means of the ritual components (*padārtha*) which serve as the instruments for severing the bonds (*pāśa*) of each individual soul (*paśu*). (p. 28)

Or, by means of the instruments for worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should perform the ritual actions appropriate to the time, designated as "auspicious" (śiva). Having worshipped [the deity] from the various maṇḍalas... (p. 29)... one should not [perform] near the fire, nor the joining of the channels (nāḍī), nor the hanging down of the cords of bonds (pāśasūtra); one should do these as previously described. And then, the knower of the rules and procedures [should proceed] in this manner.

One should perform the ritual action with the intellect. Thus, one who knows the procedure for the mandala and so forth, having correctly ascertained through the intellect all the ritual actions to be performed along with their respective requirements and foundations, should properly carry out the primary rite of initiation together with its auxiliary parts by means of the principal [intellect].
As it has been said: "He who shows contempt at the time of performing the rites of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and elevation (*uddhāraṇa*)...
[omitted] ...Śiva shall certainly dwell in hell.
Thus ends [the section from] the *Dviśatikālottara* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].
In the Vṛtti, the fourth chapter is the Maṇḍalaprakaraṇa.
Now I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), which is established upon the five principles (pañcatattva).
Following the previously mentioned collection of ritual acts up to the joining of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna),

[I shall describe it] for those disciples who possess the power of the ripening of impurities (malaparipāka-śakti) and for whom the preliminary rite of consecration (adhivāsakarma) has been performed according to the established rule.

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the means for purifying the bonds (*pāśa*) and manifesting the state of Śiva-nature. As it is heard [in scripture]: "Knowledge and true being are bestowed, and the latent impressions of the bonds are destroyed; because of this conjunction of bestowing and destroying, it is called initiation by those of purified self."

To the question, "In what is she established? he says: "Established in the five principles," meaning she is established within the five principles (*tattva*). Regarding the reading "by the five principles" (*pañcatattvaiḥ*), it means one should purify her by means of the five principles. Then, to the question, "Which are those [principles]?
he says:
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well.
But how, then, is there the purification of the entire path (*adhvan*) by means of these eleven pure elements (*bhūta*)? [The answer is:
"The entire universe is pervaded by those five principles (*tattva*).
This is the intended meaning: for here, Mahāmāyā, whose form is the power of speech (*vāk-śakti*), resides in the pure resonance (*dhvani*).

Just as in other *saṃhitās*, although [the deity] exists in the form of the principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*) in succession, and even as the bestower of enjoyment for those who worship Sadyojāta alone— even while abiding on the impure path of *māyā* in the form of *nāda*— it has been stated that, in this way, during daily worship and so forth, it serves as the purifier of the external body.

The five elements, earth and the rest, which constitute the body, as well as their respective *kalās*—specifically referred to by the names of the objects they preside over—are designated by the terms "earth" and so forth; this will be stated later in the passage beginning with "Nivṛtti is to be known as earth. For it is not the elements alone that are meant here.

These [categories] are intended [to be included here], because it is impossible for them to pervade all paths (*adhvan*). For this very reason, he says: "All principles (*tattva*) are to be seen therein by the teachers. That is to say, within those very principles—from Earth up to Śiva—all principles, specifically the phonemes (*varṇa*) and mantras, are included; and these are not contained within the *saṃhitā*s.
These are to be known as follows:

*Pratiṣṭhā* pervades the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Rudra; *Vidyā* pervades the principles (*tattva*) beginning from Puruṣa and ending with Śuddhavidyā, which extend beyond [the cosmic egg] up to Prakṛti.

Above that, up to the end of the world of Śakti, Śānti is situated within the state of Śiva; however, from the world of Iṇḍikā onwards, there is nothing but the transformation of other functions into the nature of the worlds. As it is said in the *Samānatantre*:
"Nivṛtti indeed resides within the Brahmāṇḍa, established above the hundred Rudras."
Above that, however, would be the Pratiṣṭhā, which is beyond the range of the unmanifest.
Then... [the one] appointed with nectar [proceeds] to the presence of Viśveśvara. (p.

31) "That [is] the *śāntika* [rite]; thereafter, in darkness, power alone resides in the state. Now, he states that the visualization of the path (*adhvālokanam*) must necessarily be performed by the Noble One at the time of initiation:
He who, having understood these [teachings], is worthy to perform initiation—his exertion is not in vain; he shall attain liberation.

The meaning is that one becomes attached to that [practice] out of the conceit of being overly qualified. As it has been said: "If a teacher bestows initiation upon those who do not know reality, the initiated do not go to Śiva, and the teacher shall go to hell."

Therefore, it is established that the examination of the disciple is also accomplished by means [of this]. By virtue of this cessation and the other kalās, because they preside over the specific qualities within the elements, the earth and the other elements are designated by the terms "sound" and so forth; thus he says:
Cessation is to be known as Earth; Support is said to be Water;
Knowledge is declared to be Fire; and Wind is celebrated as Peace.
Beyond Peace is the supreme ether, consisting of the essence of the power beyond peace.

The supreme placement of Kuṇḍalinī is here called the "Void" (vyoma); the meaning is that it is not the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) which is to be presided over by it. Now, are these [energies] alone—containing within them all the paths—to be [bestowed] at the time of initiation? Or is there something else? To this he says: "That which is beyond" (tatparam).
It is peaceful and imperishable. Having known that, O Mahāsena, even one who is established [in lower states] becomes fit for initiation.

It is supreme, tranquil, free from passion and the like, and imperishable. Being devoid of dimensions and other such attributes, it is the supreme Śiva-tattva, which, by virtue of presiding over all the paths (adhvan), [having] indeed extracted [the soul] from the bonds such as Nivṛtti and the rest—

The disciple is to be united by the ritual act known as *śivasaṃyojanā*. Having thus understood that very [disciple] to be Śiva, one should initiate even immobile beings (*sthāvara*); this is for the purpose of demonstrating excellence (*atiśaya*). Even a mountain should be split with the head for the sake of such excellence; [this applies to] even immobile beings.

He is capable of initiating [others]; how much more so those whose impurities have reached maturity... [he initiates] suitable castes, but not those of his own lower [caste], because a descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is possible for them [only when they are superior]. Thus, having demonstrated the pervasion regarding the scope of initiation, he now presents it in reverse order.
Understanding that Śiva’s arrival is imminent, the venerable *Svāyambhuva* scripture, through nine verses, sets forth the initiations according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*):
"One should [withdraw] *nivṛtti* by means of the heart alone, *pratiṣṭhā* by the head... [and so on].
One should perform the rite of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) with the crest-mantra (śikhā), and the rite of pacification (śāntika) with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should perform the fire-oblation with the Prāsāda mantra into the supreme ether, which transcends tranquility.
And thus the initiation, devoid of birth and the like, is completed.
However, practitioners are not liberated merely by performing the oblation (*huta*), because [the requirements for] fuel and so forth will be explained later—
either according to what is stated in the *Samānatantra* or as described in other *Saṃhitās*. After performing the rites beginning with the worship of Vāgīśvarī up to the end,
one should subsequently perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of supreme purification (*paramaniṣkṛti*) for the sake of the primary rite, [employing] the *kalās* such as Nivṛtti and the rest.
The sequence here is as follows: one should perform the rites beginning with the *hṛdaya* [mantra] in order, one hundred times each;

thereafter, one should perform the ritual actions from the severing of the fetters (*pāśaccheda*) up to the final extraction (*uddhāra*). This alone constitutes the primary ritual action (*pradhānakarma*) here due to its connection [with the goal]; however, those which are subordinate are the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) because of their connection [to the primary].
As it is stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra:
"Initiation is the purification of the impure; its constituent parts, in brief, are conjunction, enjoyment, separation, and projection, along with their equipment."
This same sequence applies even in the *Samānatantra*. As it is said therein:
"Whatever one should conceive as the *tadyonī*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the heart-syllable (*hṛd*), according to the proper order;
[and] worship, sprinkling, and striking, just as before. (p. 33)
Furthermore, restoration, joint ownership, and deposit immediately follow that.
Then one should perform the worship (*arcana*) as well as the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*),
birth (*janana*), authorization (*adhikāra*), and enjoyment (*bhoga*). Likewise, O Six-faced One, one hundred oblations should be offered with the *svatantra* [mantra] according to the *Svatantra*.
Then, one should perform the severing of the bonds with the Astra-mantra and subsequently offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
"In this case, the extraction [of the disciple's soul] should be performed by means of the heart, following the proper sequence. Thus,

having first worshipped Vāgīśī with the Adhāra-śakti and offered three oblations as prescribed in other scriptures, he should take hold of the disciple through the rites of striking and so forth, and establish him within his own self.
Having joined [the soul] with Vāgīśvarī and performed the rites from conception (*garbhādhāna*) up to dissolution (*laya*) by means of three oblations alone,

having extracted [the soul] with the *hrāḥ* mantra and offered one hundred oblations each, and having performed the severing of bonds (*pāśaccheda*) and their burning as prescribed in another *Saṃhitā*,
he should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the dismissal of Vāgīśī, and the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

In the seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), having offered the fee to the Lords of the Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*), one should uplift the disciple, place him within the body of Bhagavat, and offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). In this manner, the ritual action should be performed for each principle (*tattva*) preceded by the act of conjunction (*sandhāna*). Furthermore, regarding the fetters (*pāśa*), after the definitions of impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*, as well as that which pertains to *māyā* (*māyīya*), [the following applies]:
In the initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), which is characterized by the severance [of bonds] through the cessation of obstructive karma, there is no lack of delight;

and in the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhakadīkṣā*), even the power of mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*) is not to be purified. And it has been stated that this [initiation], being divided into the worldly (*bhautikī*) and the final (*naiṣṭhikī*) and so forth, as well as the "with seed" (*sabīja*) and "seedless" (*nirbīja*) types, should ultimately extract [the soul]. This is stated elsewhere.
To demonstrate that this is the primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*), he reinforces the very point already stated:
"For each one, a hundred [oblations] are to be offered; one should offer hundreds.
For the sake of purifying each individual bond (*pāśa*), such as *nivṛtti* and the rest, one should offer a hundred oblations for each. Thus...
The meaning has already been stated that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of five hundred oblations in this primary rite, and that the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is also included therein.

Consequently, the demonstration that even the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and so forth constitute the very nature of initiation is established because these [factors] produce the fitness for it; and here, subsequently, the offering of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed. And as for the *pūrṇāhuti*...
One should perform [it]. Now, the conclusion itself is reached: "the initiation is completed," even though it is devoid of birth and so forth;

here the word "api" (even/though) expresses negation, as in the case of "separation" and so on. Consequently, the initiation itself, being devoid of the rites such as birth which have not yet occurred, is completed in the manner of liberation. But not...
It should be explained that [the practitioner] is afflicted by birth and so forth; for in their absence, it would follow that there is no need for atonement.
As it is said:
"By means of the oblation alone, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth. They are liberated.
It is also stated in the *Samānatantra*:
"When these have been purified, O child, one attains the full ritual procedure."

This very [state] is the dissolution of the aggregate of consciousness for those two who are alone; because of the absence of transmigratory existence, it is like *māyā*, being devoid of birth and so forth. By the restrictive emphasis that "there is no [attainment] through anything else whatsoever," he rejects the notion that knowledge (*jñāna*) and other such factors are the causes of liberation (*mokṣa*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "From this bondage set in motion by that which causes obstruction, initiation alone liberates; it leads one upward even to the abode of Śiva."
The definition of the essential nature of birth and so forth has been demonstrated by us in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*;

therefore, it should be understood from that very source. And thus, for the sake of strengthening the state of Śiva-nature which has been afflicted by the bonds, there is the severing of the tuft (*śikhā*) which consists of the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*).

(As stated on p. 35: One should perform the union with Śiva as will be described hereafter, the non-hearing of that [instruction] due to incompleteness as taught in other scriptures like the *Vandhyāśāna*, and the dismissal of the sacrifice once the power of the site (*vāstuśakti*) has been attained.
Furthermore, this ritual of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) must not be revealed to one who is unqualified for it, but only to one who is worthy and has been duly consecrated by oneself.
He says it must be given:
"This which has been seen is not to be disclosed; it must be guarded with great effort.
This is the secret of all tantras, the supreme consecration."

"Regarding the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite)... [as stated previously]... it is not only here [in this specific system], but rather, it is the secret initiatory rite (*dīkṣākarma*) pertaining to all Tantras that one should strive to understand; it is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) taught for the bound soul (*paśu*) which cleanses all fetters (*pāśa*).
It does not, however, have as its fruit merely the exhaustion of karma like [the fruits of] knowledge and so forth. For this very reason...
Furthermore, since he alone has the authority in this matter, the sequence of his consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should also be observed here from the *Samānatantroddeśa*.

Now, it might be argued that knowledge (*jñāna*) and the other [means] are heard of as being the instruments for liberation; however, that is not correct, because impurity (*mala*) is a substance (*dravya*), and [it can only be removed] by another through the very activity of the Lord (*īśvara*). And within those [means], there is the reality (*vastu*) beginning with Śiva.

Only one who has been initiated has the qualification regarding the objects [of practice], such as knowledge and so forth. For this very reason, he stated that it is logically consistent to speak of the conceptual nature of knowledge and the rest here in relation to mantra-initiation.
Thus, for one whose impurities have been purified through consecration, the state of Śiva arises with certainty.

Thus, for one who has been purified by the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and has indeed been united with Śiva, the state of Śiva—which consists of omniscience and omnipotence—is definitively produced; it does not belong to anyone else who has merely been assisted by knowledge and so forth. This is the meaning. Because of this [state], it is said that there is only the state of being "liberated through pure consciousness" (*vijñāna-kevalatva*).

"Except in the case of the possibility of liberation (*kaivalya*) in the worlds above the principles of *guṇa* and *tattva*, [liberation occurs] through the exhaustion of karma by means of knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or through experience" (p. 36). Furthermore, "birth" here refers to the manifestation of knowledge and action regarding all objects within this very [world], and not otherwise.

It has been stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that there is either the prior arising [of Śiva-nature] or the transference of the attributes of the Supreme Lord—beginning with the passage, "That which is called 'bestowing' is one's own very existence," and so forth. Now, one might object: since Śiva-hood is manifested through the removal of bonds (*pāśa*), why is it described by another name consisting of "union with Śiva" (*śiva-saṃyojana*), as if it were merely the removal of a covering, like a cloth?

Just as the power of the eye becomes fully operative only when it is free from collyrium that obstructs its function, so too the power of the Self, though its bonds have been withdrawn, does not manifest objects everywhere without the reinforcement of power consisting in union with Śiva; thus there is no contradiction. For this very reason, "union with Śiva" constitutes the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Out of a desire to know, he asked:
"O Lord of Gods, abandon elaboration; tell me in brief that by the mere knowledge of which one liberates bound souls (paśus) in an instant."
