In this context, since it is already established by the statement "one should subsequently offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) consisting of the external ritual activity," that internal operation by which the teacher liberates the fettered souls (*paśu*)— making them manifest as Śiva— is what is called "unification with Śiva" (*śivasaṃyojanā*).
"Speak in brief regarding the rite; explain how one liberates bound souls (paśu) through the application of the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā).

[The opponent asks: "But how can there be these two meanings for this very same sentence? Otherwise, would there not be a division of the statement? [The author replies: "In that case, since it consists of instruction, even the simultaneous explanation of a single meaning therein is permissible."
This is seen in the Śrīmadraurava and other scriptures. Therefore, here [is] the answer to the question: "By a single effort alone, there is meditative absorption (samādhi).
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the reality by which liberation will certainly come to pass."

"O Six-faced One, ascertain correctly according to reality that practice by which liberation is certain; for he who applies himself with heedfulness is said to be one who acts in accordance with the sacred revelation. Thus it is said:
"One should join oneself through the practice of yoga to the state of the reciter."

Because the agent (*yoktṛ*) has been introduced [as the subject], it is taught that the self of initiation (*dīkṣātmā*), having become one with the Self of the Preceptor (*ācāryātman*) through union with the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*), is for the purpose of uniting [the disciple] in the state of Śiva. That [agent], consisting of wind (*vāyumaya*),

whose nature is the vital breath and the *nāda*, is the essence of knowledge (*jñānātmā*)— known by the knower of mantras (*mantravid*) as being divided by distinctions such as the "with-parts" (*sakala*) and "without-parts" (*niṣkala*).

The wise teacher, whose nature is like that of a palace, having understood through the subtle, divine path of yoga seen in the Yoga-shastra— divine because it is uninterrupted within the central channel (madhya-nāḍī) and natural because it is the means for practice—
by means of the sequence of yogic exercises such as meditation (dhyāna) and concentration (dhāraṇā), and having grasped it with a state of equanimity toward both friend and foe;

By means of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) which flows through the sensory object, because it serves as the instrument for yoga, and which is assisted by the recitation and contemplation of mantras,
through the practice of the equinox (*viṣuvat-prayoga*) born from the grace of the Śiva-teacher,
one should abandon the locations such as the heart and the causal principles such as Brahmā and others, and [reside] in that which stands at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).

In the eternal state of supreme Śiva, one should unite [the disciple] with the Fullness (Pūrṇā) externally; even in the initiation of knowledge, the preceptor who knows the mantras, having directly realized the individual soul— which consists of vital breath because it is the locus of the vital breath and is delimited by the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka)— by means of the path of yoga through the thread of the Self, unites him [with that state].

Having understood the mantras whose presiding deities are the Self, as well as the lotus-channels of the earth and other elements characterized by qualities such as sound, liberation indeed liberates; thus, according to the sequence stated in the *Samānatantrokta*, one should first purify the forms of *nivṛtti* and the others in the locations starting from the heart by means of five or more upward thrusts (*udghāta*), following the sequence of abandoning the causal levels.
By means of the *viṣuvat* practice,

one should unite the disciple with the supreme state (*paramapada*). Furthermore, he states that even in both cases, there is no deviation from the fruit of liberation for one who has attained the supreme state:
But having attained yoga according to the prescribed rule, who would not be released from bondage?

If this is so, when there exists such a means to liberation as knowledge and the like—which is accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and takes the form of the *hautra* ritual and so forth—who would engage in it? As they say:
If one could find honey right here on the branch, why would he go to the mountain?
When the desired object has been attained, what wise person would act otherwise?

That is not so, because this [initiation] has a specific object. When the power of grace (*śaktipāta*), which has reached maturity through the inference of devotion and other signs, has descended upon the minds of disciples by means of an Ācārya who is himself possessed of knowledge and intent on the performance of ritual action, the duties of the *hautra* and initiation (*dīkṣā*) are to be performed. For a disciple who is extremely sinful, whose impurity is excessive, and who is destitute, there should be the practice of yoga in extreme solitude.

One who has directly realized the reality of Śiva and other such principles through skillful means— that person established in the inner self (adhyātman)— should perform the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā).
Thus [ends the section] in the work composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand verses.
The Chapter on Initiation (*Dīkṣāprakaraṇa*) in the Commentary on the Illustrious *Viṃśatikālottara*.

Thus, the section on the duties to be performed by the initiated disciple (dīkṣitānuṣṭheya-kāṇḍa) and the section on the conjunction [of mantras] (saṃpātaka) are included therein; furthermore, the section on the initiation to be performed by the preceptor (ācāryānuṣṭheya-dīkṣā-kāṇḍa) is called the section on the knowledge of Dharma (dharman-jñāna-kāṇḍa). Regarding the optional rites (kāmya-viṣaya) for both the preceptor and the practitioner, first comes the instruction on the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) for the sake of application toward the internal state (bhāva).

I shall explain this subtle wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) in due order. This wheel of channels about to be described—which is subtle to its very core—I shall explain as it is established, beginning with the bulb (kanda). He says that very thing: *This subtle wheel of channels I shall proclaim in succession. This wheel of channels to be described, which is subtle to its very end... as it is situated, I shall explain according to the sequence starting from the bulb.* (p. 39) He says that very thing:
"Below the navel is the *skanda* which resembles a coral sprout;
it is the support of all the channels (*nāḍīs*) and is presided over by the *haṃsa*.
Thus, in that [place], the channels—being like sprouts of the tree of the body and being the cause of its function—are hollow and jewel-like.

The channels for the flow of wind, lymph, and blood have their roots in the stomach; emerging from there, they remain centered at the navel. This navel pervades this entire body on all sides, reaching as far as the pores of the skin. Moving upward, they carry [substances] upward; moving downward, they carry semen, urine, and feces; and moving obliquely, they circulate throughout.

Pervaded by the radiance of blood and other fluids, these ten principal channels are situated like a wheel in the center of the body. He explains that the usage "nāḍyaḥ" (channels) or "nāḍyaḥ" (feminine dual/plural) is seen in both forms:
"Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third."
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and Pūṣan are likewise.

"Kūrmā-kūrma" (the tortoise-like) is an elliptical expression for both opening (*unmīlana*) and closing (*vinimīlana*). "Kṣuditaṃ kṣutaṃ" (the sneeze that has been sneezed) refers to the body of nectar; "Dhanañjaya" means the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, assisted by the effort of the *ahaṃkāra*. Alternatively, the group of winds beginning with *ṛ* and ending with *ra*, situated within the heart, is the wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*).

The wind, which is the foundation of exhalation, inhalation, and coughing, causes the chest to tremble and shatter; though eternal, it takes on a transient and slight birth. In youth, it brings affliction to the young man, and in childhood, like a wheel that has turned, this singular wind sports with all elements through various deaths. (Śloka)

This group of winds which was previously released, established within the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) situated in the channel-wheel—that very same [group], being established in the channel-wheel, is supported by the heart and placed within the heart; the meaning is that it has also spread into that yellow lotus (pīta-lātāra). Furthermore, the chest...

p. 40) Regarding the word *adha*: furthermore, there is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) honorific treatment and a state of being [the object] of the Vindhya mountain. Therein, he who breathes is the "Breather" (*śvasana*);

that which is the primary vessel (*bhasta*), by virtue of its sovereignty, is the wind previously mentioned known as *prāṇa*. They say that this is eternally like one of little birth. For it is said: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) have exhalation as their limit. Nevertheless, he himself is indeed young.

The meaning is that it does not decay through actions. And this [self], which is eternal and imperishable, consisting of five aspects—whether in youth, in childhood, or even in old age—is [perceived] through sighs, breaths, and coughs; and though she was unable to move due to trembling and reeling, she suddenly experienced that bodily movement, the reeling and whirling, while remaining still.

Overcome by the auxiliary karmas and due to his insentience, Śiva plays with all beings through His power. Of what nature are they? They are characterized by "shaking" (vidhunana) deaths; because of their association with the word "death," "shaking" is the cause of a specific trembling, consisting of the emergence from the narrowness of the womb (*yoni-saṃkaṭa-nirgama*). In the *Tantra*, "shaking" (*vidhunana*)...

The meaning is: "by those who possess death," i.e., by those for whom death exists. Having thus concluded this incidental discussion on the wind and the collection of winds, he returns to the subject at hand:
"I shall describe to you in its entirety the entire wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) exactly as it exists."
Just as a single ten-spoked wheel is raised up by its divisions.

This indeed is the primary [wheel], because it is composed of ten spokes and so forth; thus it is a ten-spoked wheel (*daśāra-cakra*). And regarding its division, the meaning is that one should understand it according to the sequence of the ten locations within the *jīva*, since movement is impossible for the self due to its all-pervasiveness. In that regard, because it revolves like a bird (*cakravat*), the *jīva* [moves] through the ten locations in succession; however, because the self is omnipresent, actual physical movement is not possible. Thus, [it is called] *jīvana*.

By the word "ātman," the subtle body known as the *puryaṣṭaka* is meant. And that [subtle body] of this wheel is rotated like a wheel within its ten locations in the channels— namely, the eight situated in the eight directions and the two, one upward and one downward— by means of the vital breaths (*iṣṭāḥ*) that move sequentially.
p. 41) ... "How could it be so?"—this is the *utkrānti* (the departure of the breath) that must be known.
And this very thing should be understood as the concise practice (*saṃkṣipta-prayoga*) for the recitation of the mantra called *viṣuva*. Therefore, what is said in the present context?
Its extent is never otherwise;
that, in brief, has been declared by me to be the life-force of the world of living beings.
For its function is to be understood as the internal application of that which is called "prāṇa" through the activities of the body.
Therefore, what is said in the present context?
"Expansion is performed"—the expansion of that *vāyu* (vital air) is performed, not of a child, nor of the *śārīryātman* (embodied self).

The author of that [work] previously declared that the Self, having entered the *puryaṣṭaka* through the division of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is the "living one" (*jīva*) of the world of living beings; this is what was taught by me.

Now, in connection with the conclusion, he describes the procedure for recitation (*japa*), which is an external means required by yogins and not yet mentioned: [The verse follows: *praṇavaṃ prathamaṃ kṛtvā...* etc. (as per the source). (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, so the translation reflects the available portion.)
That which is uttered by Śiva himself, abiding within his own body,
is called "japa" by those who know the reality.

Because Śiva, though residing within this body, is as pure as a drop of water on a lotus petal and is not a mere individual soul (*puruṣa*), but rather—without depending on any other collection of causes—manifests his own nature as the previously mentioned subtle *nāda* and sounds forth by himself; therefore, for those who possess the nature of internal recitation (*antarjapa*) known to the knowers of reality, he alone is said to be the living being (*jīva*). Of that very [being]...
He states the number of days, nights, and months as delimited by the *prāṇakalā*:
"Twenty-one thousand six hundred."
The lord of yogis who performs the count of recitation within a single day and night—
Since the internal subtle self consists of days and nights (*ahorātra*),

and since three hundred and sixty of those constitute a *ghaṭikā* which in turn constitutes a year, the external arrangement of days and nights is established by sixty of those [years]. Therefore, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred flows of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
"Number" refers to the pervasion [of the mantra] during recitation; the accomplishment of that number [ensues].
Thus ends the chapter on the Wheel of Channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) in the Commentary on the *Dviśatikālottara*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme true nature of knowledge,
by the mere realization of which one no longer takes on a body again.
In this context, by the word *jñāna* (knowledge), the temple (*prāsāda*) is first denoted in the sense that "one knows by means of it.

Through the intended non-difference between the signified and the signifier, Śiva is expressed by the word *vijñāna*. Furthermore, since knowledge is of the nature of cognition (*jñapti*), the Self (*ātman*) is also intended by it. Therefore, the possibility of these—the Self, the temple, and Śiva—[being one] arises.

I shall proclaim the ultimate truth (paramārtha), by the mere knowledge of which one does not take on a body again. The meaning is that through this thorough understanding, liberation is achieved without obstacle for those who have been initiated.

But surely, [one might object], only one who has been initiated by a knower has the qualification [for liberation] based on knowledge alone. Furthermore, it has been stated that because impurity (*mala*) is a substance, its cessation occurs through knowledge alone, just as a cataract is removed from the eye.
He states the two-fold state of these three [impurities] according to their division into *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts):
Abiding in the body, He is to be known as *sakala* (with parts); devoid of the body, He is *niṣkala* (without parts).
Accessible through the instruction of a realized teacher, He exists as something indefinable everywhere.
As long as consciousness remains established within the body, the person perceives everything; however, when,

through the state of Śiva’s impelling resonance (nāda), he is situated at the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) and his consciousness becomes entirely unconditioned, then he is identical with the partless (niṣkala) Śiva.
The meaning is that he becomes capable of performing the cutting of the bonds of *dharmopāsa* and so forth. As he will state:
"That teacher who, situated within the pinnacle of the lotus of the temple, performs initiation, shall attain union with Śiva together with his disciples."
And that partless (niṣkala) nature of His is understood solely through the instruction of a realized authority and from scripture itself.

For this very reason, even in the state of bondage, the temple [of the body] remains situated within the physical body; yet it is manifested as consisting of nothing more than the forms and measures to be described hereafter.
Thus, transcending the "with-parts" (sakala), its form is something indescribable, assumed by its own will and abandoned of all sequential order.

There is no designation by means of form, for he exists as undivided by manifoldness; yet he who possesses both forms is known through scripture. If this is so, by what means and in what manner can the Lord, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), be known?
To this, he says:
"He who says 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa'—the Haṃsa is the god Sadāśiva.
He is obtained directly from the mouth of the Guru as the one whose face is turned in every direction."

The sound *haṃ* is the inhalation (*prāṇa*) of the breath, by virtue of its nature as the function of *prāṇa*, while the sound *sa* is the exhalation (*apāna*) by virtue of its nature as the function of *apāna*; for it is established that these are inseparable from the function of speech. Through this very process of the breath's movement, at every moment, according to the previously mentioned method of recitation, one should perform the invocation "I am *haṃsa*, I am *haṃsa*."

The word "brūyāt" (he should speak) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). As they say: "In contraction and in expansion, the *haṃsa*... [is] the pair. Therefore, by that [mantra], which has perished [as a separate entity], the two powers of speech and breath—consisting of the nature of speech—are recited by a person possessing knowledge through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) which denotes Śiva.

By means of the letter *sa*, which denotes power (*śakti*), because it is the expressed object (*vācya*) of the [letter] *ha* (which signifies Sadāśiva), the body of Sadāśiva’s power is obtained as being "with parts" (*sakala*). As they say: "That which is well-known from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), they declare to be his wheel.
Furthermore, through the power of yoga, it is obtained as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As it is stated in the *Anubhavatattva*: "That..."

"By means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one whose intellect is secluded and who has attained certainty through discernment, having ceased all mental construction (*bhāvanā*) regarding the form [of the deity], should contemplate through innate experiences. Or alternatively: "From the mouth of the speaker of his own qualities, through the application of his own seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the [appropriate] mode, Śiva, whose nature is existence, is directly attained; when that body has perished..."

It is said that the Puruṣa does not reside merely as the presiding controller over the movement of the vital breaths; rather, because of his sovereignty, Śiva also resides there as the impeller of that movement: "Just as oil is inherent in sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in flowers."
p. 44) Of the Puruṣa... it abides both externally and internally.

Because it is the subject under discussion, the term "Śiva" is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Therefore, the intended meaning is that for one who possesses knowledge, the realization of the Self occurs precisely from the body once [the ego] has dissolved.
Now, when the meditation on the partless (niṣkala) arises—[is it not so?]—that which serves as its basis, namely the knowledge and realized wisdom (vijñāna) of the whole (sakala)...
He says that it dissolves:
"Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard the object after having illuminated it,
so too, having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should discard the knowledge."
That by which something is known is "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Because it is the means (*upāya*), it encompasses all objects (*sakalaviṣaya*), like a flame grasped within a bundle of grass.

The partless (*niṣkala*) is that which is subtle in this world, such as shadow, fragrance, and so forth; having attained that, one should know the part-whole (*sakala*) flowers and other things which serve as the means. Fragrance is the partless aspect of that very [flower], while the tree is the whole.

The entire [manifestation] arises from the shadow of the aggregates (*skandha*), while in the world, the partless (*niṣkala*) subtle shadow—the fragrance—is established as having parts (*sakala*). That [shadow] does not exist... in form; rather, the meaning is that you alone are the entire [cause], such as the flower and so forth, which serves as the means for attaining that. And thus, by way of being both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*akala*)...

Everywhere indeed... I am Śiva among all sentient and insentient beings, established both externally and internally as the accomplisher of each respective purpose, existing as both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
There is no such thing as a fragmentary state of being that persists within the cycle of transmigration.
Pervasion is the digit of Śiva; there exists no presiding deity other than that. Thus [it is said].

And therefore, the Knower [perceives] the differentiated within the differentiated, and likewise the undifferentiated within the undifferentiated. Just as will be described regarding the forms and so forth associated with the *mātrās*, and in the employment of the collection of mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, the differentiated exists as the denotable object (*vācya*) within the differentiated temple; however, in the undifferentiated—which transcends that—the effort, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the sound (*dhvani*) abide in the undifferentiated.

And one should know this: therefore, through the *sakala* (with-form) and other means (*upāya*), one proceeds toward the means of the *sakala-prāsāda*; and for the sake of the attainment of the *niṣkala* (formless) and liberation, [one proceeds] in the *niṣkala*.
Thus: "Indeed, there are those of three measures (*trimātra*), two measures (*dvimātra*), and likewise one measure (*ekamātra*)."
"That which follows the half-mora is subtle; even half of that is the supreme beyond the supreme. Thus [it is said].

Then, the vowel *A*, consisting of three morae (*trimātrā*) and eight digits (*kalā*), is the waking state (*jāgrat-avasthā*); it is manifested through effort by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and causes the effects of paralysis (*stambha*) and delusion (*moha*). The vowel *U*, consisting of two morae (*dvimātrā*) and thirteen digits, is the dream state (*svapna-avasthā*); it is intensely manifested by the vital breaths and so forth, and involves burning, placing, and other such functions.

Even though the single *kartṛ* consists of only one *mātrā*, it possesses eight *kalās*; situated within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), characterized by intoxication (*mada*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, it is the generator of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and other such effects. Likewise, the fourfold *bindu*, which consists of half a *mātrā*, remains as long as it is manifested through the very subtle vital breath (*mandatara-prāṇa*) and the like; it is the cause of delusion (*bhrama*), paralysis (*uccāṭana*), and other such results.
Half of that is half a *mātrā*, from which [arises] the one called *daśārdha-kīkalaunā*, the means for the attainment of yoga and isolation (*kaivalya*).

These are said to be the long, protracted, long-short, and short *mātrās* associated with the consonants. By means of the syllables of the *praṇava* (such as the letter *ca*), the syllables of the *prāsāda* mantra are joined. And thus, together with that—
When the six measures (*ṣaṇmātra*) are being uttered, they become half-measures (*ardhamātra*) by way of the nature of the path (*adhvan*) of the entire temple (*sakalaprasādaka*).
Then, becoming partless (*niṣkala*), their movement is withdrawn and they dissolve into that which is called *Kuṇḍalinī*, the supreme material cause (*paramopādāna*).

Because its essential nature is the supreme material cause and because it is the agitation of the power of Supreme Śiva (*paraśivaśaktikṣobha*), it is "supreme" (*para*); yet, because it is also the half-measure, it is "supreme-and-non-supreme" (*parāpara*).
It has been stated:

"By these two, respectively, Śiva is to be approached as both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*)," concluding that there is the realization of His true nature. This applies not only according to the sequence just mentioned, but also to [the deities] beginning with Brahmā, whose essence consists of the vowels such as *Ā* and so forth.
The state described as "with parts" (sakala) and "without parts" (niṣkala) is stated even according to the sequence of the abandonment of causal factors:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva—
she who consists of these five deities is recited as being "with parts."
The Brāhmaṇa is the heart, Viṣṇu is stationed in the throat,
Rudra is situated in the middle of the palate, and Maheśvara is in the forehead.
One should know Śiva to be at the tip of the nose, and beyond that, the Supreme beyond the supreme.
"There is nothing higher than the Supreme"—this is the certainty of the scripture.

And since these locations have been described as having the forms of waking and so forth in succession, the touching of the location is established after the utterance of the *sakala* (manifest) *prāsāda*. Thus, for the one who utters that *niṣkala* (unmanifest) state— which is said to be higher than the highest— at the *dvādaśānta*, there arises pure consciousness.

Here, the fact that [this practice] is the cause for attaining the supreme state (*paramapadaprāpti*) is also made known. In this context, because the space between the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*) and the tip of the nose (*nāsāgra*) are equivalent, the term "tip of the nose" denotes the state of being a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*). Therein resides Śiva in his state of authority (*adhikārāvastha*); and therefore, those things situated within that [state]...

The forms beginning with waking have been described in sequence; thus, after the utterance of the *sakala* (manifest) *prāsāda*, there follows the touching of the locations (*sthāna-sparśa*) and the state of becoming partless (*niṣkalī-bhāva*), like a perfected being (*siddha*). Because that [mantra] has been declared as "higher than the highest" (*parātpara*), for the one who utters it, upon the arising of pure consciousness (*śuddha-saṃvit*), it proceeds from the center of the eyebrows.
Because the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and the tip of the nose (*nāsāgra*) are identical, the term "tip of the nose" refers to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmavila*).

Therein resides Śiva in his state of authority (*adhikārāvastha*). Consequently, because it is immediately following that [state] and situated near it, there exists no other reality whatsoever than the Supreme (*parā*); rather, the supreme state (*paramapada*) itself is found therefrom.

There is nothing else higher than that, because it alone is the presiding authority over all... [it] brings about conjunctions and disjunctions through its powers. Even so, the meaning is that it attains a state consisting of excellent conjunction and disjunction within the locations of the channels (*nāḍī*). If it is asked by what this is caused to revolve, [the answer is] by action (*karman*) acting as a cooperative cause.
By the power of Śiva, [that] does not arise in those locations. As it is stated in the *Samānatantra*:
"Even when situated on the eastern petal, there may be a multitude of men;
and in the *tejas* [petal], hunger arises in the *viḍā*."
In the southern direction (yāmya) [he is] Yama; in the southwest (nir-ṛti), he is designated as Nairṛta;
on the leaf of Varuṇa, Varuṇa; and on the leaf of Marut, the state of Marut.
"In the north, the state is known as *saumya*; in the northeast (*īśa*), it is called *īśa*. Whichever direction one approaches, one attains that entire state.
Thus, that *jīva* is perceived by the world of living beings, yet not by those who are deluded. It is indeed this [jīva] that constitutes the earth and so forth for this world of living beings.

The individual soul (*jīva*) is to be known as having the form of a body born in the world at the end of a *kalā*. Nevertheless, because it is veiled by impurity (*mala*), it is called "the deluded one" (*mohin*) and so forth;

thus the living soul is described as the presiding principle over the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body). The Self (*ātman*) is not known apart from the body and its adjuncts. He clarifies this very point:
It is proclaimed as the *cakra* because it moves in ten ways;
it is known as the *nāḍī-cakra* (the wheel of channels) because he indeed traverses therein.

For the reason that the *jīva* moves there in ten ways, transmigrating from one station to another, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*) because it revolves like a wheel. Furthermore, that upon which this *jīva* rests while undergoing transmigration is known as the "wheel of channels" (*nāḍī-cakra*); such is the explanation... [the rest of the sentence is fragmentary].

Thus, by means of the general mark consisting of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it has been indicated that our agent, the living being (*jīva*), is to be inferred. Now, the question arises from a desire to know its specific nature:
Just as that life-force (jīva) of the world of living beings is known in its true nature, there is a great doubt in me regarding this; O Śaṅkara, be gracious.
Now, here is the reply: "O Six-faced One, listen to the vision of the individual soul (jīva) called Puruṣa;
I shall describe it to you without doubt, especially out of affection for my son."

The Self is that which is distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth... Listen to the cycle of signs (*liṅgacakra*) by means of which it is perceived. I shall explain those signs by which this body is known to exist. And here, just as worldly people [determine] specific times such as the *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign) through the inference of particular flowers and so forth, [so too is the Self known].
One should transition there. The sun is known [as the measure] of the internal divisions of time because it consists of the specific movements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (p.
48) Through the knowledge of that [sun], the individual soul (*jīva*), which is its agent, is easily known; therefore, those very [movements] are the signs (*liṅga*) here. ... not otherwise.
The transits and equinoxes, as well as the days, nights, and solstices; the intercalary month, the abortion, and the *aumarātra*.

That which was prescribed and prohibited regarding the specific times of the feet and arms of the *puṃs* [the Sun] is indicated by names in order to show that it should be performed in exactly the same way during the ten specific times pertaining to the internal state (*adhyātma*), which consist of the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*). As they say: "By name..."

Regarding the "extension of the dharma" (*dharmātideśa*), this is now the description of their essential nature: the night of *aumī* is indeed the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*); yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*) occurs here; and *jaṇat* is here... for that breath is called wealth (*dhana*).

Since the word *aum* is intended here in the sense of "deficient" (*nyūna*), the meaning is: that in which there is no night (*rātri*) whatsoever, nor anything else. For it is heard in scripture that initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and so forth, cannot be performed without poison (*viṣa*).
Likewise, the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is an increase of months; and that, in this context, is indeed yawning (*jṛmbhā*), as will be explained later.

The activity of the mind consists of the individual experience of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. As it is stated in the venerable *Trayodaśaśatika* [Tantra], in the section on the "Cutting of the Lunar Days" (*tithiccheda*): "This should be known as debt during [the increase of] *vṛddhi*, and this becomes wealth.
Therefore, in this context, wealth is the exhalation consisting of *prāṇāyāma*, because of its nature as a *pala* within that [process].
The ritual action must be performed.
Now, the definition of the solstices and so forth.
The northern should be known as the southern, and the left is designated as the right;
thus it is said that [the breath] has issued forth from the two nostrils.

The southern [channel], which has a tawny whorl and rests upon the right nostril, is the form of the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa); it is to be known as the "Devyā" and the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).

The nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the essence of Śiva’s vehicle, resides in the *vardhanī*, *āvarta*, and *vāmanā* [channels]; it is the cause of the flow of the breath through the two nostrils that enter the *suṣumnā* within the central region designated as the *dakṣiṇāyana*.
The equinox is established. And among these, the ritual action is to be performed according to one's own specific quality. As it is stated in the *Samānatantre*:
"That which belongs to the Sun... [is one], while the other is declared to belong to the Moon."
The Moon and Saturn in the conjunction of fire (the tenth house) are indeed auspicious for consecration.
"And that which begins with meditation occurs at the equinox. Also, in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:

"Having wiped away the two lords of day [the sun and moon] and [perceiving them] as they abide in the middle region, one should know that to be the equinox; knowing that, it becomes the bestower of liberation."
When that Lord of the World, the God of gods, remains in the northern course (vṛtta),
one should know this as the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) and proceed to the state of Śiva.
Just as Maheśvara abides in oneness with the moon,
one should know [that state] designated as the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
The sequence of the hands... when, having left Svāti for Himālaya, one goes from water back to fire, that is known as *saṃkrānti*.
"Having abandoned the objects of the senses and being established in the supreme ether, remaining motionless... one should designate that as the *viṣuva*. Now, the definition of *saṃkrānti*:
Furthermore, its transition occurs through the union of one position with its own respective position.

From its own place, specifically from the south, the transition of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs through union in that very same place and not in another channel. Regarding that place of the *prāṇa* where the transition is said to take place,
he says:
It is endowed with Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and Amā.
Suṣumnā is situated in the middle part of the body, Iḍā is established on the left, and Amā on the right, O Skanda; among these, it is called Tisrocyate.
The absence of lunar days (*amā*) has been mentioned here by Piṅgala. Now, assuming a more subtle internal nature of time, he states the definition of day and night:
"Indeed, the upward breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward breath (*apāna*) are respectively the day and the night. (p. 50)

For that very Sun, who is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is said to rise as a whole; however, by way of the function of inhalation (*apāna*), it sets, and thus night occurs. Consequently, through three hundred and sixty transits (*saṃkrānti*), there are the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), beginning with the primary [solstices].
With three hundred and sixty breaths, a year [is formed]; by means of an external day and night, sixty years are produced. As it is said in the *Samānatantro*:
"Alternatively, O Mahāsena, I shall tell you in brief."
Sixty years are declared by yogins to constitute a single day and night.
O Six-faced One, three hundred and sixty breaths are proclaimed to be the number of a *ghaṭikā*;
thus is the year described here, wherein each *ghaṭikā* corresponds to the external [time].
Inhalation and exhalation constitute a day and night. Thus it is said.

"He who knows these ten divisions of the vital breath (prāṇa) is truly a knower of the gods; likewise, he who knows the ten distinctions of the vital breath, such as the transits (saṃkrānti) and so forth, is a knower of the Vedas. Thus it is said.
The Vedas are so called because they know (*vidanti*) the Self, Śiva, and Śakti; he knows them. Furthermore, the Śruti is his authority.

For that Prāṇa, the breath-holding (*āyāma*) known as *kumbhaka* within the heart-lotus is the "seizing of the moon" (*somagrahaṇa*), which is meritorious; and at the twelve *samāna* points, it is the "seizing of the sun" (*ādityagrahaṇa*). This has been stated in the *Samānatantre*:
"The extension situated within the body is intended as the lunar eclipse;
however, the wise should know that which transcends the body as the solar eclipse.
Thus, it is said that the Self is to be known by means of these ten signs.

Having thus explained the internal division of time, [the author] now provides instruction on *prāṇāyāma* so that one may distinguish the *jīva* from the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— this being for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that the vital breath itself is the *jīva*.
I shall now describe *prāṇāyāma* to you in brief.

(p. 51) I shall explain [the practice] by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth. Since this has the nature of being "with seed" (*sagarbha*), he describes the inhalation accompanied by the recitation of the mantra and meditation upon its referent:
"The knower of yoga should recite the *praṇava* with a single vowel-sound."
One should fill the abdomen with air to the desired extent.
This is breath control (prāṇāyāma); it is the "filling" (pūraka), which fills the body.

Having first purified the channel (*nāḍī*), one should fill the interior of the belly with power as far as the *dvādaśānta* through the state of meditation, breath, Śiva, and mantra. One should utter the *praṇava* in a single tone (*ekaśruti*), according to the scripture: "He who knows the restraint of *prāṇāyāma*. And in the sacrificial rite (*yajña-karma*), it should indeed be the *udātta*. However, some say—

"One should not conceive of any difference between the temple (prāsāda) and the *praṇava*. By this scriptural statement, the temple is expressed by the word *praṇava*. They say that one should utter it as "na" when it is interrupted by a single *mātrā*.
And because it fills the body, it is called *pūraka* (inhalation). Now, for *kuṃbhaka* (retention):
Having closed all the openings [of the body] and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled jar; this is the *kumbhaka* breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
As for *recaka*: the knower of mantras should then exhale the breath upward with a single inhalation (*śvāsa*).
*Recaka* is the expulsion of air from the heart-lotus upward through one nostril. Furthermore:
One who is engaged in the yoga of exhalation should expel the breath upwards;
this is known as *recaka*, which can cause danger to life.
Through the inhalation of the breath via the central channel (*madhya-nāḍī*), by means of yoga characterized by the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),

and accompanied by the recitation of mantras and meditation on Sadāśiva, one should then exhale the air residing in the heart-lotus upward through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*). This, indeed, is the distinguished exhalation (*recaka*) in the Śiva-āgama.
It is particularly renowned; "one who causes danger to life" means that even a mild application [of it] produces doubt regarding one's very existence.
(p. 52) Now, he states their purpose:
That lotus which is situated in the heart and stands with its face downward indeed opens up when it is filled by the inhalation (pūraka).

The heart-lotus, which is always primarily expanded by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), thereafter becomes an upward-flowing channel; however, it is emptied by exhalation (*recaka*). That lotus, previously drawn up by exhalation—which instantly seizes the vital breath—is released from restraint by retention (*kumbhaka*) and, once expanded, returns [to its state] through exhalation.

When, by means of the practice previously described regarding the sustenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the breath] is cast upward—that is, exhaled—while moving through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), then the upward flow becomes directed upwards. And at that time:
"Having released the heart-lotus, the upward flow is established."
The reciter goes... ||
Having pierced the door of the skull, the life-force is indeed expelled upwards.

Having gone to the state of Śiva forever, one shall not undergo birth again. Thus, by means of that exhalation (recaka) which is equal to oneself, one who has been purified by it stands facing upward within the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī). Thinking "I am Śiva," he pierces the path through the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows, reaching the door of the cranial vault (kapāla-dvāra).
Having pierced the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), he is then especially exhaled upward to the station of Sadāśiva, which resides within the powers of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. (p.
53) How can there be coming and going for him, or by what means is he led?
O Mahādeva, please explain this doubt to me according to its true meaning.

Because that self is all-pervasive and formless, coming and going are not possible. Even if its coming and going are perceived by way of the door of the city of eight (the body), nevertheless, one must admit that its movement culminates at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta); otherwise—

Just as in the state of *vijñānakevala*, since the partless consciousness (*niṣkala-saṃvit*) does not arise without its means, there is no yoga of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha-yoga*) or yoga of existence (*bhāva-yoga*) in this external physical body; yet, how is it that there is a return to the body? This is the question.
And since that subtle body is insentient and the person lacks the capacity to direct the external body, by whom is it led? This is the second question.
[The answer is: The living being is led by its own power; having reached that [state], it returns.
This person is led by the power of action (kriyā-śakti) presided over by Śiva and Śakti;

or else, having reached the *dvādaśānta* once, he returns from that place as far as the heart. However, in another state, under the influence of karma, [he proceeds] when not presided over by the life-force (jīva-śakti).

Or rather, it is the power of the person to turn back [from the path] that leads to death; thus there is no fault. Now, he specifically shows the supreme state, the place to be attained by the aforementioned consciousness:
"I shall fully declare its end; listen to it in truth, O Six-faced One."
The meaning is: "I shall describe the place of rest for that *haṃsa* of the vital breath.
One should know it to be beyond the body, at the end of the *nāda*, twelve finger-breadths [from the heart];
one should recognize it as situated within, and the Lord, abiding there, pervades [all].

That which exists beyond the body, twelve finger-breadths above, is the place of rest for the *haṃsa* of the vital breath—the *ātman*—at the end of those twelve [finger-breadths], known as the *dvādaśānta*. It is the partless (*niṣkala*)...
[the state] where the sovereign Lord of Consciousness, being all-pervasive, becomes manifest in the void (*vide*). Now, [regarding this...]
He demonstrates the fruit of direct realization: (p.
54) Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eye is cast elsewhere, the yoga of yogins nevertheless proceeds in an uninterrupted manner.

Because the mind and the eye have form as their characteristic, even though they depend on the sense organs and are intended [to function] elsewhere within their own respective objects, for those knowers of the nature of Śiva who reside in the palace [of the heart], the yoga of realizing the pervasive Self and the yoga of realizing Śiva proceed uninterruptedly by the power of practice. And therefore:
The intention is that there shall be enjoyment and liberation free from obstacles.
As it is said: "Even while dwelling in the midst of sense-objects, the wise man does not dwell [therein at all].
He concludes that very point by way of another's perspective on what is to be adopted and what is to be abandoned:
This is that supreme secret; this is that supreme state.
This is that supreme Brahman; this is that supreme Imperishable.
There is no knowledge higher than this, and there is no auspiciousness higher than this.
"There is nothing higher than this," said the Blessed Lord Śiva.

The sense is that among all the other statements concerning the stations of liberation, this is the supreme; there is nothing higher than this. He demonstrates the authority of this meaning—that these aphorisms were spoken by the Supreme Lord himself and not by me—because he alone is omniscient and, due to his stainlessness, is the most authoritative of all.
May this very [teaching] established by tradition be "svāhā"!
This nectar of the knowledge of Śiva has been proclaimed in brief and not in detail;
it is the determination of the supreme syllable obtained from the Lord of the Gods of gods.

According to the scripture, "The palace is the supreme syllable" (*paramākṣara*). Wherein there exists no decay of this palace of the supreme syllable—that is this section on the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, which is the determination of the supreme syllable. And because this is illustrative, all of this knowledge has been [expounded] by me.

This has now been related in brief as obtained from the Supreme Lord. Therefore: "For this, the true essence of Śiva, which has issued forth from the mouth of Śiva, is the secret more secret than the secret... [should be preserved] with effort. (p. 55)

The word "hi" (for) is used because Śiva’s mouth is his power (*śakti*) in the form of speech and protection; therefore, this pure scripture—which has issued forth from that [mouth] and which reveals your true nature as Śiva—is your very essence.
Consequently, you too must guard this most strictly. And for this reason—
It must never be given to one who has no son, nor to one who is not a disciple;
it should be given to one who is devoted to the gods, the sacred fire, and the guru, and who is free from envy.
This knowledge should be given to him, but never to anyone else.
It has been stated that there is a transgression in giving [the gift] other than to the prescribed recipient. In the *Samānatantre*:
"The giver of this goes to hell; it is never accomplished.
And this... which I have spoken to you, is the truth, the absolute truth.
Having understood this, the wise person should move about at ease.
Indeed, having understood this nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, one whose life is knowledge becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta);
such is the meaning. For it is said:
Whether a householder, a celibate student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
wherever he may be situated, the man of knowledge is always a knower of the supreme syllable.
One who possesses sense objects and is attached to them attains Śiva at the end of the body;

[this applies] among those endowed with the four stages of life (āśramas) who are established in the knowledge of the supreme Imperishable. Having become unattached to these [stages], one goes to Śiva alone at the end of the body. It should not be explained, however, that even one who is attached to sense objects goes to Śiva.

Because it contradicts the scriptures. Furthermore: "By this very knowledge, even a human being attached to sin is not tainted by merits or sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin or the horse sacrifice."

p. 56) As soon as one here becomes superior and a knower of the scriptures, being liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) due to the absence of the impurity that is the cause of *saṃsāra*, he remains—by virtue of the karma whose effects have already begun—as a subject experiencing the external body, even though this subsequent sin might arise; this is to be explained like [the case of] a corpse. As it is heard:
"It is said that for transgressing an order, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years."
In this context, as a secondary point, the classification of teachers is stated:

"The teacher is traditionally remembered as being of three kinds on this earth: the one who impels (codaka), the one who awakens (bodhaka), and the supreme one who grants liberation (mokṣada). Thus are the three types of teachers.
And among them:
"The prompter shall show the path; the awakener shall point out the place;
but the giver of liberation [bestows] the supreme reality, having gone to which one does not return."

The *codaka* (the one who urges) is the indicator of the pure path; he should be called a teacher (*ācārya*) by virtue of being a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth, for through his instruction on awakening, he demonstrates the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—he is indeed the primary guru.
However, the bestower of liberation (*mokṣada*), who performs initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, establishes the supreme reality of the *paraguru*.

Thus ends the section on the Nectar of Knowledge (*jñānāmṛta-prakaraṇa*) in the commentary on the *Śrīmad-dviśatikālottara*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand verses.

Now, in order to explain the creation of mantras and the specific visualization (dhyāna) pertaining to internal purity and connected with *śuddhavidyā*, which serve as the means for the practitioner who has attained perfection, he says:
"In the center of fire is the station of the sun; in the center of the sun is the moon..."
In the midst of that is the divine sprout; from that, creation proceeds.

In this context, because the sequence of meaning (arthakrama) possesses greater force than the sequence of recitation (pāṭhakrama), it should be understood that the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala) is above the solar orb (ravimaṇḍala), and the fire orb (vahnimaṇḍala) is above that. These [three] are presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, respectively, and they are denoted by the words *vidyā*, *śivatattva*, and *śabda*; furthermore, they consist of action (*kriyā*).
The instruments of manifestation belonging to the power of the will of knowledge (*jñānecchāśakti*)— which are specific states of the effect-phase of the Kuṇḍalinī power,

consisting of the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and so forth, and which are of the nature of the self and distinct for each individual— subsist therein; and within that [space], [the Lord] presides over them.

By virtue of the context, that which is denoted by terms such as *kuṇḍalinī* and so forth is the Supreme Bindu (*parabindu*). At the time of creation, it first becomes connected with individual souls (*puṃs*). From that arises the *puryaṣṭaka*.
And that [Bindu] exists in a distinct state for each individual soul in the form of the pervasive instrumental faculty (*karaṇa*). Likewise, it is always present within consciousness.

It is true that, like a jar or other objects, it is preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*). For, as in the case of a sprout, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is used here [in the term *nāda*], meaning "that which has a sprout. Therefore, it is said that [the power] exists within each individual soul (*puruṣa*) in the form of the primordial sound (*nāda*), which is the effect (*kārya*) in its initial state, and subsequently in the forms of *māyā*, *kalā*, and so forth. This is what is called *nāda*.
"That which is supreme, all-pervading, and situated within all beings"— this is declared to be the Maṇḍalāgnikāṅkura.
It should be meditated upon by the practitioner as facing downward from the *dvādaśānta*, joined with the *puruṣa* in the region of the heart,
and composed within the four lotuses of peace (*śānti*) and so forth.
The wise one should contemplate his own body as having a divine form, beyond compare;
the learned one should contemplate whatever specific activity has been prescribed for him.

Although the entire world of illusion (*māyīya-jagat*), characterized by both the immobile and the mobile, is common to all and consists of fire and moon (*agnīṣoma*) because it is presided over by Śiva and Śakti— and thus possesses the nature of fire and moon— nevertheless, one's own body, consisting of the subtle and the gross, is the opposite: it is purely of the nature of the moon, the immortal nectar (*amṛta*).
One should contemplate the inferable, perfect divine form. Likewise, that which is the prescribed function of the aggregate of principles (tattvas) residing within that body—

distinguished by the divisions of pure and impure, beginning with *nāda* and *kalā* and ending with earth— is precisely the same as the function of the organs of action and so forth, such as drinking and eating.

One should lead the mind, which is of the nature of death, [to immortality]. Now, the conclusion: (p. 58) "He who practices this meditation, which is nectar facing in all directions, shall in no long time become a partaker of the fruit of perfection. Otherwise..."
Without knowing the ritual placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*), how can a practitioner apply it?

They are like fools who try to break the sky with their fists. Thus, without knowing the ritual placement of emanation, if a practitioner strives for this state of accomplishment, that effort is merely an exercise of power.
"One should engage in action that is free from calamity; thus, my knowledge must necessarily be practiced by the seeker.
Thus ends the chapter on Agni and Soma in the *Kālottaravṛtti*.
Now he describes the method of recitation (japa) conducive to the success of the practitioner himself:
"If one recites continuously after having raised the resonance (nāda) of the Prāsāda [mantra], one attains perfection within six months; there is no doubt that one becomes perfected in yoga."

Recalling the *prāsāda* mantra beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should raise the sound that consists of the path of the *śakti* through the resonance of the bell, and recite it incessantly.
The practitioner quickly attains the purification of *śuddhavidyā*. Regarding this very point, he states a specific detail:
Through the recitation of the *gamāgama* mantra, the destruction of all sins occurs;
within six months, one shall attain the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) of the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.

In this context, "going and coming" (gamāgama) refers to the recitation of the mantra as far as the *dvādaśānta* [the twelve-finger space above the head], and from that point back again to the heart (*hṛdaya*) by way of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). This is the contemplation of that time. For one who is thus engaged in the contemplation of going and coming, through the performance of recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [the purification is achieved].
There shall be the destruction of all sins.

For the sake of accomplishment, by practicing this, one attains the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇimā*. Some maintain that here, due to the context of going and coming (*gamāgama*), the *haṃsa* mantra is intended by the word "palace" (*prāsāda*). Therefore, having raised its resonance (*nāda*), [one should proceed].

(p. 59) Through recitation performed with diligent effort, accomplishment is attained without delay. They say that through the contemplation of the coming and going of the breath (*prāṇa*), there is the destruction of evil. Having understood the coming and going in both ways, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. Having become absorbed in that and having come to possess that realization...

Within six months, one shall attain perfection. The seeker of liberation who understands the coming and going of the *haṃsa* here, or the resonance (*nāda*) being uttered, or the scripture of the *Prāsāda*, is liberated. Even the practitioner, absorbed in that, becoming one with it and not turning away from it, attains success through the intellect before long.

Regarding this, the Gurus maintain that through the recitation (*japa*) of the coming and going [of breath], there is accomplishment (*siddhi*), and through the non-coming and non-going, there is liberation (*mokṣa*). That very [recitation] is described by me as the Prāsāda [mantra] in its gross, subtle, and supreme forms.
The gross Prāsāda is described by the passage beginning with "the eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group" and so forth. It utters...

By the words "by oneself" (*svayam*) and so forth, the subtle (*sūkṣma*) [Prāsāda] is indicated; by the words "partless" (*niṣkala*), "devoid of body" (*deha-varjita*), and so forth, the supreme (*para*) is indicated. However, some say that because they accomplish their respective fruits through the recitation (*japa*) performed with sandalwood powder (*pāṃśu*), mentally (*mānasa*), or as a whispered muttering (*upāṃśu*), the Prāsāda is declared to be gross, subtle, and supreme. And regarding that—those who do not know the Prāsāda do not truly know.

Śaṅkara [is he] by whom that Supreme Lord— who is the very nature of the temple (prāsāda) described above, together with its material cause and its simultaneous fruit— is understood; yet He is not understood as divided into the distinctions of Sakala and so forth, because without knowledge of the means (*upāya*) as it truly is, there is an absence of knowledge of the goal (*upeya*).
As it is heard: "One who is proficient in the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) attains the Supreme Brahman."
Thus ends the chapter on the Prāsāda [mantra] in the Commentary on the Dviśatikālottara composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand verses.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the temple (*prāsāda*).
Having thus stated that I shall proclaim the characteristics of the mantra other than those already mentioned, he asks what they are and says: (p.
60) "The short (*hrasva*), the long (*dīrgha*), and the protracted (*pluta*)—the knower of mantras always [employs] these two sets of characteristics. Among them, the short burns."
Regarding sins, it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"When a confluence of all sins has arisen,
one should mutter the five purifiers and the one [mantra] of manifold forms."
The five purifiers are indeed the Brahmans; when prolonged, they become the bestower of liberation. In that regard, it is stated:
"One attains liberation by chanting the limb of Śiva. Then, in the *Āpyāyana*, [it is said] "and so forth," adorned with the nasal drop (*bindu*) at the head.
The meaning is that the *pluta* (protracted vowel) is also the cause of nourishment (*āpyāyana*). This is stated in the *Samānatantra*:
"One should cause the nectar situated at the end of the process to flow there. This is because it is joined with the *bindu*.
Now, [one might ask] is this common to all mantras? It is stated in the *Tantra*: "It stands above all. From these...
Thus, due to the conjunction with other qualities, other results are described—

namely, subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). "Gross" (*sthūla*) refers to that which is perceivable by the external senses, having the nature of the physical (*adhibhautika*) as taught in other tantras.

Or whenever it is employed, then those [mantras] produce their subjugating fruits. To the question, "What does the internal [mantra] do for them?", he says: "For even one who has leaped across [the stages] always necessarily brings this about; there is no doubt in this matter."
When joined with the long *phaṭ* syllable, it swiftly expels [the obstacle].
At the beginning and at the end of a short vowel, the syllable *phaṭ* is beneficial for the purpose of incantation (*māraṇa*).
Another application of the short [syllable] alone is proclaimed for the purpose of attraction at the beginning and the end of the Heart-mantra.

By enclosing the Heart-mantra at the beginning and the end with the short syllable, one effects attraction. However, some desire the application of the Heart-mantra at the beginning and the end of the name of the person to be acted upon. Immediately after that, he says:
Thus one should attract the person to be accomplished, having known their name. So it is said.
Now, would this [power] attract only what is proximate, like a magnet and so forth, or even that which is distant? To this he says:

(p. 61) "When properly applied, one may certainly attract [the object] even across hundreds of leagues. Thus one should attract the *sādhya*; it is not [attainable] by one who does not know the reality of the Name."

The practitioner who is disciplined and devoted should not only bring near women and others who are already present, but even those who are far away, established in another place of vision, for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. He states the reason for this right here:
The *bindu* (vital point) of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is superior, while that of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is said to be inferior.

Wherever the fire of the practitioner [is stronger], success belongs to him; immediately upon seeing it, the other becomes accomplished. Therefore, it is established that a preeminent practitioner of power shall attract a preeminent object to be accomplished by power.
Now, the conclusion: Having understood this, the wise practitioner certainly performs the attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
Without knowing this correctly, the practitioner does not achieve success in rites for the gods (*daiva*).

Having thus understood the distinction between the application [of the mantra] and its isolation, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the two goals to be accomplished by oneself, one should draw [the deity] forth. That is to say—for instance—the meaning is that one should grant the twelve-fold refuge and so forth, provided one has the capacity to do so.
Now follows the procedure for the practitioner’s duties (*kartavyatā-vidhi*).
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should cause the mantra to be pervaded;
then, having performed the consecration (sekam) of the mantra, the wise practitioner should perform its recitation (japa).

Having performed the previously mentioned mandala sacrifice, and having consecrated [the disciple] with the water from the jar presided over by Śiva as prescribed for the mantra to be mastered, one should recite the mantra to be mastered after offering the first half of the mantra for the sake of purifying the body: "Having consecrated oneself by means of the Self, O Ananta..."
Victory comes from this: the practitioner of mantras should observe the mantra-vow according to the path prescribed for the mantra of the one to be accomplished (sādhya).

Furthermore, this recitation of mantras and so forth belongs to one who has been consecrated for the mantra to be accomplished; the consecration of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should be examined in another treatise. Moreover, he should remain established in the five characteristics within the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
At the conclusion of the recitation, there should be a ghee oblation of ten thousand offerings;
thus nourished, the mantra then becomes fit for ritual action.
Regarding those rites which have been described, their accomplishment is certain;
having worshipped the Liṅga of the Supreme Lord and the like, and having taken recourse to His Dakṣiṇāmūrti form while seated upon the lotus-seat at the right face of the Deity.

"One should worship the subtle form of the *sādhya* within the light of Aghoralocana"— according to this scriptural injunction, having performed the worship of the *sādhya-mantra* on the lotus-seat of Śiva at the right face, one should complete the count of five hundred thousand recitations by adding the daily counts together; finally, [one should perform] the worship of the maṇḍala.
Having performed this, one should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with a *sruva* ladle using the mantra of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Thereupon, the rites prescribed for that [mantra] will be successful. Alternatively, at the end of the daily recitation (*japa*), a fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed in accordance with that same number. From this very recitation, when endowed with other qualities, [the results follow].
He states other fruits:
"Whoever recites [the mantra] one million times, the inhabitants of Janasthāna will surely come under his control; this is the certainty of the scripture."
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand and five hundred times, the inhabitants of ten villages come under one's control,
along with their wealth and even their very selves.
Having recited thirty [mantras], one should bring the stainless [state] under control;
he who recites thirty-five will bring the earth under control.
Thus ends the chapter on the Prāsāda [mantra] in the commentary on the venerable *Dviśatikālottara*.
In this regard, following the etymological derivation of the word *jñāna*, Kārttikeya himself poses a question: (p.
63) "O Lord, O Master, even now there remains a doubt concerning knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
How is it that this is known as 'knowledge'? Or rather, let it be told how the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is to be understood."

That by which something is known here is the instrument (*karaṇa*), namely form (*rūpa*); and that which is the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*) consisting of cognition (*vijñapti*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because all [these] have not been explicitly stated, there is doubt regarding their distinction. Furthermore, is that instrumental cause, knowledge (*jñāna*), of the nature of cognition (*jñapti*) or not? If it is of the nature of cognition, then [the definition] is "knowledge by means of a hundred."

The question is: "If [the two] are of the nature of satisfaction (*tṛpti*), how is that known? Furthermore, just as between the cognitions of Caitra and Maitra, their mutual awareness of one another is untenable. Here is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"But having first known the supreme substratum (*ādhāra*), the conceptualization of the superstratum (*ādheya*) follows after."
The wise man who understands the relationship between the support and the supported is competent in all actions.

That by which one studies is the *ādhāra* (substratum); it is the means (*karaṇa*), namely knowledge. Having first performed that, one must subsequently produce the conceptual knowledge (*kalpanājñāna*) of the object to be established—the *ādheya* (the supported), which is the self (*ātman*) in the form of the object of attainment (*upeya*).
Since she is eternal once that means has been discerned and known... [the individual] who does not know the Self is a bound soul (paśu) dependent on karma. Now, what is that knowledge of the means?
It is said that the city, which is the support, consists of the nature of consciousness (vijñapti); the one who resides therein is called the Lord (Īśa), and he is the establisher of the supports.

That which consists of knowledge (*jñānātmaka*) is called a "city" (*pura*) because it is related to the intellect (*buddhi*), like a city, and because it is the locus of experience (*bhoga*). Furthermore, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it is that by which things are known; the meaning is that its nature is pure consciousness (*jñapti*). Some say here that by the word "city," the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) itself is meant. As for the object to be contained within it, it is established as the Self (*ātman*).
The Lord's status as the enjoyer of that [fruit] is stated as follows:
"Indeed, he who is the master over the eightfold group within this [universe] is remembered as its Lord (Īśa)."

Because she rules as the sovereign (*īśānī*), she is called *Īśī*; she is the power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyāśakti*). Below that, within this body, she attains [her state] by being the agent who employs the means of experience (*bhogasādhana*).
She is remembered as the culmination of purification (*śodhyavasānā*) for knowledge, which consists of the determination regarding what is to be purified (*śodhya-vyavasāya*). From that...
The wise man who, having realized this, always rejoices within himself,
even while joined with the subtle body of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), moves both downward and upward.

Having known that which is called the "City of Eight" (puryaṣṭaka) as being eternally blissful, and having realized the Knower of that intellect—the Lord whose nature is the Self—the wise one proceeds upward for the sake of perfection, both to the full extent of the body and beyond;
no other does so. It is stated here that the bound soul (paśu) lacks such qualification.
Now, regarding the true nature of that "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka):
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—this is remembered as the city of eight.

Here, the group of effects is indicated as twofold: the five elements and the five subtle elements (tanmātras), which are comprised without distinction by their own qualities such as sound and the rest; likewise, by the word "five" [in the fifth category], the two groups of instruments known as the organs of perception and the organs of action—numbered as five—are included within the internal [group] by the terms beginning with "intellect" (buddhi).

The group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) and the group of sounds (*śabdavarga*), which here consist of the manifestation of qualities (*guṇa-vyakta-ātmaka*) arising from their respective locations; the group of primary natures (*tat-prakṛti-varga*) consisting of passion (*rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), and the rest; and the group of coverings (*kañcuka-varga*) consisting of *māyā*—these are declared to be the groups of supreme nature (*para-prakṛti-varga*). Thus, within this city of the external body and so forth, there is a sequence of eight groups of atoms (*vargāṇu-krama-aṣṭaka*).
It is recorded [in scripture].

Now, an objection: is it not the case that the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), consisting of thirty principles from earth up to time, is well known as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)? This [subtle body] is impure, being the means for wandering through the pure and impure worlds.
Its essential nature is likewise well-known. As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:

"This quality of the principles (tattva-guṇa), beginning with the earth and ending with time, which is determined for each individual, wanders according to karma through all bodies, O Lotus-born One."

In this context, however, because even the *bindu*, which is the effect of the pure essential nature (*śuddhasvarūpa*), is said to reside within all beings by way of the *nāda* and thus serves as the cause for supreme liberation, at the time of departure (*utkrānti*),
the entire category of principles (*tattvavarga*), both pure and impure, is designated as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) of everyone.

Although he has been liberated from all fetters through initiation (*dīkṣā*), nevertheless, as long as he is not released from these bonds by means of the initiation that grants immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*)— which interrupts the experience of the fruits of karma already set in motion— that very bondage remains until the end of the existence of this body, which lasts for a hundred years and is constantly pursued by those [fetters].

Therefore, for the sake of ultimate liberation from them, these [objects] must indeed be abandoned once they are understood in the context of the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*) and so forth. Now, he describes the sequence of abandoning those very objects: "One should abandon sound and touch, because this sound has space as its object, and because of what arises from air."

The sound (nāda), originating from space and air, issues forth from the body and reaches the mouth; thus, by means of the throat—the locus of Keśava—one should abandon the sense of taste, because that [taste] has its root there. As Patañjali said:

In the throat alone hunger and thirst are ceased; in the palate one should abandon form and smell, because that [palate] is the root of the faculties of form and smell—thus it has been said: "one should enter smell into the palate. In this way, the abandonment of the two groups of effects is stated in their own respective places, as in the expression "one should abandon [them] in Brahman alone," and so forth.

The purification of the gateway of the *samaya* through the seedless initiation (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*) consists of the renunciation of such things as sound and touch— which are of the nature of the sense organs presided over by deities such as Brahmā— for the sake of avoiding their impairment;
and because this [initiation] is characterized by the equinox (*viṣuvat*), it takes the form of the abandonment of all fetters and has *utkrānti* (the upward departure) as its objective.

The mention of "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "ego" (*ahaṃkāra*) is merely illustrative... one should abandon even the station of the Lord (*īśvara*), which transcends the group of five. In this context, "mind" (*manas*) refers to *māyā*, for it is the locus of authority over the effects of *māyā*.
(p. 66) And the "drop" (*bindu*), as well as the pure primordial nature (*prakṛti*), constitute the Great *Māyā* (*mahāmāyā*) within the station of Sadāśiva.
Having abandoned [the body] above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one becomes equal to Śiva, liberated from these sins.

Thus ends the chapter on Knowledge and Realization (*jñānavijñāna-prakaraṇa*) in the Commentary on the *Dviśatikālottara*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].

(p. 67) ... [In order to show that] these must be performed at the appropriate time and not otherwise, he states the procedure for the *kālacakra* for the sake of knowing the signs of death (*ariṣṭa*) and so forth:
"I shall explain the procedure for the *kālacakra* in due order."
That which is renowned as the *Kālacakra* is so called because it is understood through time;

since the regulation of internal time is established therein by means of the gateway of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), I shall explain that specifically. Furthermore, that *Kālacakra* is already well-known by its essential nature in the time previously mentioned. Thus [it is said]: "by which..."

One awakens at the proper time through the regulation of internal time, which is not explicitly stated [elsewhere]. Regarding this, it is said: "By means of the movement of the *iḍā* for a day and night... [it] flows. Indeed, by the movement for two days and nights, one lives for two years."
By moving for three days and nights, he lives for one year.

As it was stated previously—"The upward breath is indeed *prāṇa* and the downward is *apāna*, and [the former] is night"—one should cause the flow of that internal day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Its measure is stated to be sixteen *truṭis* for each; therein, that single flow of *prāṇa* is also [to be understood] as such.
One should practice with the visualization of the elements (*bhāvavarṇa*). One should apply focused attention there for as long as the flow continues within the channel or until it ceases.
For the sake of the realization that delimits the aggregate, or for the sake of awakening... [or] the aggregate.
Through the deception of time, one should practice the retention of the deceased (*mṛtadhāraṇā*). By means of the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], whose moon has waned...
The determination [of time] consists of the departure [of breath], the practice of application, and the intermediate *māyā*, as well as the movement according to one's will;

thereafter, within the measure of the internal day-and-night (*ahorātra*) consisting of sixteen *tryuṭis*, there is the movement characterized by its upward departure. The nocturnal movement is that which has the form of the upward-moving breath (*ūrdhvaprāṇa*).

The digestive fire (*pāka*) also occurs [in this manner]. He lives for three years; however, it should be understood that he whose measure in the body is double [the standard] lives for two years, while he whose is triple lives for only one year.
This sequence for examining time, pertaining to the internal [self], has been declared for those who possess knowledge.

Some teachers maintain that the full comprehension of time must be achieved by means of the measures of days, nights, and so forth, through the flow and movement of the *nāḍīs* starting from the beginning. Because its movement occurs there [in the body], it is demonstrated specifically in that context. First, they mention three words: "He who, without knowing the word... and so on.

One should examine only that channel which flows externally and internally. Then, due to the flow in the aforementioned channel, one should know that the result is merely the seeing of a hair. Now, if it flows for two days and nights...
having determined that the lifespan is two years, if one were to grasp [the breath] during the time of sacrifice for the retention of death, [it would be successful].

Deception should be practiced. If there is a determination [to renounce], one should spend the remaining time by relinquishing all possessions and so forth, and then effect the departure of the vital breath according to one's own will:
"One may practice for a single day, or even for a single night."
His death shall occur within six months; such is the certainty of the scripture.
One should practice for two watches of that [night] during which one lives through the day and night.

In this case as well, regarding the perspective of time, the meaning is quite clear: for one whose movement and return occur at the very same time as the day, or at the same time as the night, he lives for a full [period]. But he who exists only after that time lives for exactly one day and night (*ahorātra*). This is not to be understood merely through the flow of the *iḍā* [channel]; furthermore—just as:

It has been stated that this is to be known by the movement in any one of the channels— namely, the left (*vāmā*), the right (*vāmā*), or likewise the middle (*madhyamā*). Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other portents (*ariṣṭa*) mentioned in other scriptures,
such as [the non-hearing of] sounds, the failure to grasp the scent of books, and bad dreams.
Now follows the conclusion:
The Kālacakra has been fully explained out of special affection for my son.
Thus ends the section on the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*) in the commentary on the *Kālottara* in twenty [verses].
