Just as elsewhere it is a secret that pleasure arises from the union of a husband and wife— a reality accessible only through one's own solitary meditative concentration (*ātmaika-samādhi*) and impossible to convey to another through mere speech— so too, the knowledge of Śiva and other [deities], when not contradicted, results in a pleasure born of the objects of the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-guṇa*), which is to be personally experienced.
To demonstrate that it cannot be revealed by any other speech, the Lord spoke the section concerning Bṛhatkumārī:
"Just as between a young maiden and her lover, when they are established in mutual affection..."
One woman is united there, while the second shall suffer misery.

While a mature woman and a maiden remained together out of mutual affection, the latter, distressed by her failure to obtain the lower [sexual] position despite being joined by a single garment, said first:
"O blessed lady, that pleasure which you shall speak of from union..."
I shall speak, O blessed lady; there will be happiness in the Dharma.
The second one said: "Having seen and embraced that [woman] again, you were filled with longing; what was previously indicated by you, speak that now. The first one replied:
"I am unable to say that which you desire to hear."
The second one said: "Then he spoke in anger: 'Why have you acted thus, O you who are false to your promise?'—the meaning is: 'Why have you now done this, you whose vow was true?
Then, having obtained her desired pleasure, she [the first wife] appeased the angry second wife... such and such."
Because there is no cause other than the means [of union]:
O blessed lady, that pleasure which arises from conjunction does not arise otherwise.
It is because they speak of it otherwise that it is said to arise from a [specific] causal condition.
Therefore, that very reality cannot be explained at all to one who is unenlightened.

Since that bliss, which consists of joy born of union, cannot be compared to any other pleasure whatsoever, it cannot even be described; rather, it is to be experienced only through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedya*).
Otherwise, I shall speak of it as it is taught in the first scripture...
That which was previously indicated by you is exactly so, there is no doubt;
and whatever was spoken by me as a kindness out of ignorance and the delusion of pleasure, [that too is as you said].
Therefore, forgive me, O blessed one; as before, accept me as your beloved.
Therefore, it is established that Śiva is to be approached through any one [of these means], just as the taste of clay is [experienced through its smell].
Thus ends the chapter on the Narration of the Virgin (Kumārikākhyāna) in the commentary on the venerable Viṃśatikālottara.
Now, here is a question arising from a desire to know the Prāsāda [mantra]:
"The division of Śiva has already been promised as being eightfold;
O Lord, please explain it out of your grace."

Just as previously the difference in results was stated to arise from the recitation of the *prāsāda* mantra according to its divisions into short, long, and protracted vowels, so too has the eightfold division of this [mantra]— consisting of *śreyasī*, *arimā*, and so forth— been promised to yield results through its recitation.
As it is said:

"One shall attain the sovereign power of the qualities such as *aṇimā* within six months. This statement regarding the variety of fruits applies also to the distinction between mantras; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [The mantra is] with parts (*sakala*), without parts (*niṣkala*), void (*śūnya*), enriched with digits (*kalāḍhya*), empty space (*kha*), and rendered pure (*amala*).
They know the eighth [consonant] to be the *kṣapaṇa* (the destroyer), which is the *kaṇṭhyoṣṭhya* (velo-labial).

Because it has the nature of destruction (*kṣaya*), this nasal (*anta-stha*) sound is called the "nasal of destruction" (*kṣayam-antastham*). In that regard, the definition of the whole [mantra] is as follows:
The temple (prāsāda), joined with the sixth and endowed with the six additional [elements],
is proclaimed as the Śiva-tattva, which is complete and resides within all beings.

Here, by the word *prāsāda*, the interior [of the temple] is meant. That [interior], when joined with the sixth vowel *u*, and endowed with the final letter of the sixth [vowel], *apavarga* (*a*), which has been transformed into an *anusvāra* (*m*), is called the *sakala* Śiva-principle; it is proclaimed as such because it possesses all [aspects] (*sakalatvāt*).

As it is stated in the venerable *Trayodaśaśatika*: "The sixth vowel of this [syllable] ends in *su*; the letter *ha* together with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) shines forth. And that is within the *mūṣṇi*; all this is the true being (*sadbhāva*). And because it is to be pronounced with great effort, it is called the essence of all beings. He characterizes the partless (*niṣkala*):
He who, having abandoned the body, departs by himself—that is Māruta;
one should know him to be Niṣkala (partless), Śiva devoid of the six phonemes.

The Śiva-mantra with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), which was previously described starting from the words "the eighth seed-syllable from the preceding group" and so forth, is that which— when accompanied by the six syllables beginning with *ā* (the five ancillary syllables and the syllable *oṃ* denoting Śiva) placed above the mantra— is devoid of the "own-hand" (*svakara*) mentioned in the same Tantra and is joined solely with the seed-syllable *jā*.

It becomes "partless" (*niṣkala*) because it has been born. For this very reason, that essence of resonance (*dhvanyātmā*), through the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), gradually abandons its state of having parts and emerges by itself. As it is said in the venerable *Trayodaśaśatika*:
"The Lord Śiva is partless; He is the peaceful one, conjoined with the wind."

But he who explains that even by means of the syllable *au*, [the breath] is beneficial only after having struck down [the body], contradicts the stated scripture. Now, the definition of the Void (*śūnya*):
Having pierced through inhalation and exhalation, it remains within bodies like a piece of wood.
One should understand that it is empty; one should contemplate it with the heart.
The meaning is that one should recognize the form of the plow (*halākāra*) during the state of *kumbhaka*.
As it is said in that very same [text]: "Empty, like a broken arrow, crooked in shape like a serpent, soundless, devoid of ego, without appearance, and free from desire."
And one should contemplate that within the heart with the mind. Regarding the "Kalāḍhya" (Abounding in Parts), it is said:
That which is heard on earth as uttered from a mouth shaped like a kiss—one should know that to be Kalāḍhya. ... [omission] ... ||
Just as in the case of a beloved’s kissing and so forth, the two outer lips [are joined];

by means of a face shaped like a bud, the *śivatattva* is uttered. One should know that this is enriched with all the *kalās*. Some call it the *aghorabīja*, while others call it the *īśānabīja*; it is enriched with all the *kalās*.
Those learned in the true scriptures say it is a palace (*prāsāda*). As it is stated in that very same work:
"Whatever qualities are said to belong to the *sakala* [deity], those same qualities belong to the *kalāḍhya* as well;
having understood the first vowel to be thus 'existent' (*sat*), [one should know] its successive [states]."

"Because of its union with these syllables, it is remembered as superior to the totality [of the universe]; since it is surrounded on all sides by the *kalās*, that Śiva is remembered as *Kalāḍhya* (Abounding in Parts). Thus [it is said].
He said that the earth has been made [into] space; listen to my [explanation] of what is proclaimed as the end of the upper resonance when it has subsided.
One should know that the space situated therein has been made impure.

When the *nāda*—which is accompanied by the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), which is luminous, and which, being attenuated, dissolves through the process of [the phoneme] *kāra*—reaches its end, that is the *mātrā*. Through the examination of this, the supreme *oṃkāra*, situated in the space of the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*), is rendered complete by means of that very sound. One should know that when it is uttered, the void (*kha*) is rendered complete; and that...
"Some say it is Sadyojāta; others say the seed-syllable is in the heart; the Gurus say the seed-syllable is in the head.
One should know that the leader of mantras is the pure void (kha), situated in space, joined with the letter *m* on all sides, adorned above with the bindu. Thus [it is said].
He describes *kṣapaṇa*: "But having heard the Lord, the Teacher of the World, with averted face, it is called *kṣapaṇa* because it is the cause for the exhaustion of suffering."

(71) [Thinking] "May it arise," one who has heard this from the Lord Śiva and grasped it with his ears, because it is a counteragent [to obstacles], should utter the Lord in that very way—specifically ending with a *saṃ* (the *sānta*)—and recite [the mantra].
And because this serves as the cause for the destruction of suffering for one who thus recites it, it is remembered as *kṣapaṇa*. Some say this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Aghora.
Others say it is the syllable *kṣa*; the Gurus say it is the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdbīja*) itself. As it is said therein:
"One should oneself utter it with a turned-back mouth as if it were in one's own mouth... [divided by the vowels] in the form of a mendicant (*kṣapaṇaka*)."

One should utter the first [vowel] with a long sound; such indeed is what is called a semi-vowel (*antastha*). Now, that which is established at the end of the exhausted nasal (*anūda*)—one should know that as a semi-vowel, proclaimed as being unutterable.

Furthermore, one should know that the end of the *prāṇa*—which consists of the activity of drinking the *nāda*, which has become exhausted and dissolved into its support—is established as the internal limit (*antastha*). Because every syllable is non-different from the *nāda*, there is simply no further production upon its exhaustion. This is true. Therefore, that [the *prāṇa*] is not its cause; rather, it is another, namely the *apāna*.

Alternatively, because it is to be pronounced as entering within—preceded by the space (visarga) of the path known as *vṛtti*—it is called "internal" (*antaḥstha*) and "reddened" (*ārakta*) due to its being the gateway; thus, it is also proclaimed as "not to be pronounced," and there is no fault. Furthermore, some maintain that in this context it is simply [the letter] ending in *s*.

The teachers, however, say that because it is not heard [in the scriptures] as being among the inner-stops (*antastha*), and because it serves both purposes through *tantra* (economy of effort), it is the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astra*) itself—namely the *visarga*—which, when uttered thereafter, is considered an inner-stop (*antastha*). In that very place where it is said to be "ending with *sa*" (*sānta*), "destroying" (*kṣapaṇa*), and "resting" (*viśrama*), its location is found to be completely dissolved (*saṃkṣīṇa*). Thus, it is called the "destruction of existence" (*bhavanāśa*).
Regarding the throat and lips, he says: the eighth of the eighth group is the peak; the second of the seventh;
that which transcends the groups and ends with six; and the fourth of the third in the seventh.
Furthermore, the first [syllable] should be joined with the sixth, and indeed the sixth with the first.
The eighth is remembered as the letter *kha*, joined with the crest (*śekhara*), [placed] on the throat and the lips.

From the *mātṛkā* consisting of eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*), one should first extract the seed-syllable called "ha," which is at the end of the eighth group starting from the eighth lord; then, one should place beneath it the second letter of the seventh group, which ends with "ra.
Next, one should take the syllable "kṣa" which transcends the groups, the final "ma" of the sixth group, and the third letter of the seventh group.

One should join the fourth *lakāra*, the first *vakāra*, and again the *yakāra*. Then, one should join the sixth vowel of the first [group], which is *ūkāra*. Here, by the word "kha," which denotes emptiness (*śūnya*), the syllable that expresses the *anusvāra*—the *bindu*—is meant. By means of that *śekhara* (crest) situated above, [one joins] the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and so forth.

Because it indicates the measure [of the vowels], it is rightly remembered by Ananta and others as the ninefold *kaṇṭhoṣṭhya* (the gutturo-labial), which is to be uttered with a single effort. Now follows the conclusion.
These divisions have been fully described as the means for attaining *aṇimā* and the other [powers].
Because they establish the various forms of Śiva presided over by the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) and others, these divisions are like limbs;
and because of the inclusion of the names of the eight accomplishments (*siddhis*) beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as other accomplishments.
They become practitioners; it is prescribed that one should not utter the poison of the eye.
Furthermore, that which is the nature of *nāda*, not yet having attained grossness and flowing as sound, is also described hereafter for the sake of recollection as the means to liberation.
Thus ends the chapter on the exposition of the eight divisions of Śiva in the commentary on the venerable *Dviśatikālottara*.
Now, as an incidental inquiry regarding the very nature of sound:
How is it pervasive? And how does it exist below, above, and across?
O Maheśvara, out of compassion, tell me this true state of being.
(On page 75: "That which is called Nāda, the supreme seed-syllable (bīja), exists from the very beginning within all beings.

It has been stated in the immediately following chapter that the pervasive Nāda—by means of the passage beginning with "of the exhausted upper Nāda" and "of the exhausted lower Nāda"—moves both downwards and upwards; and how is that so?
It might be argued that because this is a property (*dharma*) [of the body], it would not be all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*); for this very reason, its pervasiveness has been stated.
It is true that the object established by the mantra has been shown therein; thus the meaning is understood. The question is:
as long as a living being remains in the body, he is proclaimed to be "below" (*adhaḥ*).
The portion within the heart pervades transversely, while that [which is] situated inside pervades everywhere.

Because it remains distinct from its substratum, the living being, that sound (*nāda*) never [becomes manifest] here; as long as it abides within the body in the form of *nāda*, it does not exist below, above, or across—so it has been said. From the moment it emerges from that, having transcended the state of being an effect, it remains as the internal, non-causal state.

Then it pervades everywhere—horizontally, upwards, and downwards. And thus, the practitioner who does not know the being situated in the three paths within all bodies shall not be liberated, even if this dissolution occurs.
Although there are indeed three paths, the vehicles (yānas) are likewise threefold; however, that which is called the Śiva-vehicle does not exist therein. How so?

Because one who knows the Supreme Nāda—which resides within all bodies as the nature of the effect—and becomes absorbed in it through initiation and other means, attains the accomplishment of the practitioner (*sādhaka-siddhi*)... [in] whom.
Even all those who are obstructed by the impurities of office that oppose their application, as well as the spiritual sons hindered from liberation,
are liberated because they are pervaded by that [divine] knowledge.
Having thus spoken by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he speaks by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*):
The three paths and the three foundations exist within all bodies;
those who know this pervasion will undoubtedly attain everything.
He who thus follows along as the self of the effect within all bodies.

p. 76) Having understood that this [universe] is the locus and support of those situated on the three paths—the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantramaheśvaras—just like a pearl released from its string, he knows this aforementioned pervasion as belonging to that very Cause-Self (*kāraṇātman*). He himself is all-pervasive and liberated from all supports.
One who knows the true nature [of reality] becomes Śiva; as it is said:
"He who is proficient in Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman.
Having thus demonstrated the pure nature of Nāda and its fruit, [the author now describes] the pervasiveness of the knowledge of the Self.
In this context, he states the result as a corollary: "One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find pervasiveness;
having known the all-pervading God, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt."
By whose grace one does not find a life similar to that [of the liberated],
meaning one does not obtain it nor makes it an object of experience; for so long does he wander in saṃsāra,
but having known the pervasive Lord— the self whose nature is luminosity— even from this sound (nāda), he is undoubtedly released.
The meaning is that his fruit of initiation shall proceed without obstacle.
This very point is explained by means of an illustration:
"Just as a caterpillar or the like, having reached the tip of a blade of grass..."
Just as that [ether] above is without support, so too does the individual soul (jīva) abide here.

In the state of *saṃsāra*, because knowledge and action are obstructed by impurity (*mala*), the manifestation of that which expresses them—the effects and instruments—does not occur; rather, since they are manifested only after knowing something [through them], one’s perception of this [Self] occurs through those very [instruments]. And thus, just as a leech moves from one blade of grass to another...

That very blade of grass is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of this self; thus, through the three meditations characterized by upward, downward, and horizontal [movement], he performs that function of the instruments and so forth. [The text] states: "The living being (*jīva*) resides here," meaning it exists within the body. At that time, even his own true nature (*svarūpa*), due to exhaustion...

The meaning is that he considers [the self] to be merely the size of the body. And thus, being unbound by knowledge of the nature of the all-pervasive, he who understands the void above, the supportless, the triple-void (triśūnya)—O Guha, he is certainly eternal. This is the nature of the Self according to the stated sequence.

Above sensation, below, in the middle, and across—in these locations characterized by the emptiness of the self—it shines forth as the stainless state of saṃsāra, not as a skin disease... one does not know the mantra-emptiness of the self as being free from affliction; rather, one knows it through its state of being devoid [of such]. Everywhere, there is only emptiness.
The meaning is that he knows. That initiated one is certainly liberated. Thus, in this way—the pervasion and the rule have been declared in brief, but not in detail.
Beyond this, [is] the attachment to... which is the ripening of the pervasive one.
Since there exists nothing further beyond that which constitutes the pervasive Self’s own nature— which is not pervaded by anything else—

because it is pervaded by the Lord; therefore, from the word "māyā," [it follows] the beginningless and endless pervasive Self, and likewise Śiva, who is of the same genus as that and follows after it...
And in this section as well as in other sections, the pervasion has been stated in brief.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on Pervasion, in the commentary on the Kālottara in twenty-two [thousand verses].
Having thus demonstrated the incidental pervasion of *nāda* and the rest, [the author now speaks] regarding the subject at hand:

"Henceforth, I shall explain how the eightfold realization (*pratyaya*) comes about for the practitioner when it is directed toward his own state, having bestowed liberation upon the officiating teacher through the purification of bonds."
The future and the prior [conditions] are eightfold; I shall explain how the condition and the state of being become knowledge. As to what these are, he says: (p.
78) "I shall explain the blazing of fire as well as the seizing."
It is the paralyzer of fetters and the destroyer of great sins.
The equinox, the rendering seedless,
as well as the destruction of the planets and fever— these are the eightfold signs that manifest spontaneously.
Likewise, the equinox (*viṣu-saṃkramaṇa*) is the leading of the power (*śakti*) here through its withdrawal.

When this is known according to the rule, renown arises everywhere. Thus, for one who knows the eightfold set of convictions (*pratyaya-aṣṭaka*) according to the rule, success arises through correspondence with the results in all actions where results are observed. And here, it is complete...

Having received the mantra through a traditional lineage, the Guru or the practitioner— having performed the preliminary rites, being without fasts, having bathed, and wearing white garments and ornaments— should worship Śiva in a pure place marked with a svastika;
then, with a steady mind and intellect regarding the purpose, and for the sake of all signs of success, this is the first application therein:

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ. The Praṇava joined with the letter *ra* is Sadyojāta; Śiva is between two *ra*s, and Sadyojāta again joined with *ra* followed by *namaḥ* is for the kindling of the fire. These are to be employed in the Agni-srotas [rite] accompanied by a thousand recitations.

By means of the application of the five-syllable mantra, [the enemy] is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt. Having first prepared unimpaired fuel there, and having recollected the evil mantra in its entirety, one should recite it according to the procedure of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, [causing it to be consumed] by the stream of fire through the flow of the *piṅgalā* channel and the movement of the *udāna* breath for a thousand [breaths].
One should apply [the mantra] there as far as possible. This is an illustration; it includes the presence of water and so forth.
In that context, the distinction is that the *sākāra* (the letter 'a') and others are joined with the *repha* (the letter 'r') of another mantra.
Now, the second [mantra]: ŪṂ HRŪṂ HRAUṂ HRŪṂ VONNAMAḤ.
The seed-syllable of Śiva is situated within; [the practitioner] should perform obeisance while remaining established in that state during the examination.

This is the Yoga of the Tulāpuruṣa, which is proclaimed as a rite to be performed according to the rules for the purification of great sins (mahāpātaka), using the upward breaths (udghāta) and the unshaken [mind].
When, even during its growth, no heaviness whatsoever arises;

For the purpose of the expiation that destroys the great sins (mahāpātaka), there is the production of another heavy substance equal [in weight] to that which was superimposed as the determinant; the application is: "Uproot it for the sake of the destruction of that sin."

Oṃ hyāṃ hyauṃ hyāṃ oṃ ………… The seed-syllable of Śiva is likewise whirled by the wind; similarly, at the end of that [seed-syllable] is "oṃ," and "namaḥ" at the end— this mantra effects the destruction of sins.
Furthermore, regarding his re-initiation, lightness arises for that sinner through this mantra; by the re-tying of the matted locks (*jaṭā*), lightness arises from the destruction of sin.
Now, the fifth [topic]:

Oṃ hyaṃ hyauṃ oṃ namaḥ. Tāra (oṃ), jīva (ha), and sa (sa) with prāṇa (ha), conjoined with Śiva (u) and Vāyu (ya); preceded by dhīra (oṃ) as before and followed by adhoṅkati (namaḥ)—this is for the destruction of poison.
This is the mantra for the yoga of neutralizing poison... [the] yoga [is accomplished] by eight hundred *udghātas*, according to some. Now follows the sixth application:
likewise in the non-kindling of fire, and similarly in the rendering [of the body] seedless (*nirbīja*).
A specific distinction is prescribed here by means of five hundred upward breaths (udghātas).
(80) Especially for the purpose of neutralizing portents, wrestling matches, and blazing fires? Now, the seventh [mantra]:
Oṃ hrūṃ hraṃ hrūṃ phaṇṇmaḥ.
p. 81) ... *yutasāgni* Śiva, and again *sāgni* Śiva;
then the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *phaṇiti* at the end, for the mind [situated] in the mouth that ends with the *ghṛhāṇa*.
And thus, in this practice, he separates [the breath] from the flow by means of the equinox;
with eight hundred *udghātas*, he swiftly and certainly destroys the house.

The eight-fold ritual action: *oṃ hāṃ phaṭ oṃ hāṃ phaṭ oṃ hāṃ phaṭ*... *phaṭ phaṭ*. Here, the *tāra* (oṃ), *śiva* (hāṃ), and *phaṭ* at the end constitute the mantra; with fire, the fruit is obtained, and the mountain (na) follows.
As before, the branch consists of five *phaṭ*s; one who sacrifices thus is the destroyer of fever.
This application, however, should be performed by way of the gentle path. Now follows the conclusion:
"I have thus described the application of the eight means of realization;
having understood them thoroughly, the best of teachers should employ them according to the prescribed rule."

Thus ends the eighth chapter on the Means of Realization (*pratyaya*) in the commentary on the *Śrīmad-dvīṃśatikālottara*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand verses.
Again, a question concerning the palace:
of what nature is the palace to be known, and of what nature is its pervasion? Of what nature is its manifestation? Tell me, O Maheśvara.

Is it not the case that, because the temple was previously raised by the thread called *nāda*, it is well known through the description of the short extraction (*hrasvahṛti*) and so forth? [This is] the question... for this very reason, this is a doubt concerning another existence.

Since it has been stated that "the Sakala is to be known as residing in the body," and since this [term] *sakala* denotes Śiva (p. 82), it exists both as the source of the five Brahmans who constitute His body, and as the designator of the power (*śakti*) presiding over the causal lords such as Brahmā. Therefore, with the desire to know its specific nature:
The question: And therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) must indeed be consistent with that.
[He] who does not know the temple, whose great body consists of the five mantras—
One who is not endowed with the thirty-eight arts is not called an Ācārya.

Having understood both Śiva and the body of power (śaktiśarīra)— which consists of the five kalās beginning with Īśāna, is joined with the production of effects, and extends to the end of the Prāsāda mantra— as both the signifier and the signified, one becomes an Ācārya.
The man who performs initiation without correctly understanding the temple leads both his disciple and himself downward; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, that teacher who bestows initiation while stationed within the heart-lotus of the temple spire shall attain union with Śiva, together with his disciples.
The temple (*prāsāda*) itself is the lotus, because it is that which is presided over by Śiva; thus, it resides within the body.

The sound (*nāda*) of the protracted pronunciation (*plutoccāraṇa*) of the temple is consciousness (*saṃvit*) residing at the unconditioned *dvādaśānta*, conjoined with the body through the activity of Śiva. This is the meaning. According to the scriptural statement, "His powers are equal [to Him]," *sāyujya* is the state of being together (*saha yugbhāvaḥ*).
"Of equal power" means up to that point. "Possessing union with Śiva" (*śivasāyujya*) means that this [disciple] has union with Śiva;
the state of that, the Guru, that seeker of Śiva (*śiveṣya*), attains. By that very [means], having the form of the five mantras... [the sequence is:
Ādhāra, Kala, Prajāpati, then Āditya, Śukra, Skanda, and likewise Guru. Those who also...

And all the palaces (prāsādas) should be spoken of; the seeker of liberation and the practitioner do not falter in their state of being. These and many other sages of firm vows meditate upon the supreme Haṃsa, known by the name Prāsāda, which is the Supreme.

(p. 83) The meaning is that they meditate upon it by reciting it as the name *Prāsāda*, because it denotes that [deity]. And this *Prāsāda* in the form of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) constitutes the body of Śiva. It has been stated that, by virtue of denoting specific powers (*śakti*), the thirty-eight [deities] consisting of the five mantras arise therein. And in that regard—

And I shall explain its "homogeneous" [aspect], by knowing which one attains deathlessness; for it was already promised that I would speak both for the sake of meditating upon what is to be expressed and for the sake of the specific realization of the expresser.
One should know that the left [face] arises from the syllable *u*, endowed with eight digits (*kalā*),
while Aghora arises from the syllable *ma*.
The Bindu is to be known as Puruṣa, while Īśa is born from the Śikhā.
In this way, the mantras are traditionally held to be produced from the Prāsāda [mantra].

But these are not the syllables of the *praṇava*, such as *a* and so forth; nor are they the syllables of the *prāsāda*. For it is true that those [syllables of the *prāsāda*] begin with *hi* and so on. Therefore, here, because the syllable *a* has arisen within the truth (*satya*), the syllable of the *prāsāda* produced therein—which is called the syllable *ha*—is [identical to] the syllable *a*.
The origin of Sadyojāta... is also heard [in scripture].

"The letter *a* and the letter *u*, these two, when established as one—therein no separation exists, just as between the wind and the sky. Thus, the meaning is that [the syllable] is born from the letter *a*. ... The application of the *praṇava* at the beginning of the mantra is established.

Immediately, the [deity] endowed with eight *kalās* is the object of worship. Even Vāmadeva and the others are to be meditated upon as forms distinct from Sadāśiva according to their respective distinctions of *kalās*. Thus, he says that through the knowledge of the Prāsāda [mantra], all the mantras presiding over that which is pervaded by it and worshipped as Śiva become worshipped: [The text continues: "By means of the knowledge of the Prāsāda, all the mantras presiding over that which is pervaded by it and worshipped as Śiva become worshipped. He states this as follows:
Of thousands of tens of millions of weapons of immeasurable power,
there is no doubt that they will become desirable to you in the palace, even if they were not previously desired.
[Objection: But surely seven crores of great mantras are heard of; how then is it said that there are "hundreds of thousands of ten million"? To this he says:
"Those mantras proclaimed as the Mārutas, Sanakas, and so forth..."
All those born from the lotus of the palace possess unfailing power.

The meaning is that for those who are stainless (*nirañjana*), there is a finite enumeration, whereas for those with stains (*sāñjana*) and others, the mantra is indeed infinite due to its dissolution.
As it has been said:
"Other mantras belonging to Pradhāna, such as those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth, are inferior."
The meaning is: "Those with *sañjñā* (consciousness) are situated in the middle, consisting of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* natures.

Furthermore, in this context, the word *mantra* primarily denotes that which has the nature of reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*). However, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it is applied to the denoting word itself. Consequently, other *mantras* [are related] to Śiva, who is the denoted object (*vācya*) of the temple (*prāsāda*).
When employed as mantras, the expressive sounds— which consist of the constituent parts of the temple and are produced from the primordial source (*anāda*)—
become the designators of their respective objects of expression.
Now, Viṣṇu is indeed Brahman himself, the presiding lord over the aforementioned causes and so forth.
It is said that this body is to be presided over by means of the door [of the senses].
Indeed, the Lord Maheśvara himself is the true God;
even for those who worship the nature of the Brahman-mantras such as Sadyojāta and the others in their purity, Śiva alone is the world of Nivṛtti and the other stages.

The meaning is that it must be propitiated for the sake of attainment. He states that the network of sounds (*śabdajāla*), which is the temple, is to be presided over by Śiva—who is expressed by those [sounds]—through the mediation of their respective powers (*śakti*). Thus he says:
Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda;
Aghora is the Sāmaveda, and Puruṣa is called the Atharvaveda.
The fifth, which is supreme and subtle, is Sadāśiva.
Because the Vedas serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*), the entire expansion of speech (*vākprapañca*) has neither the sacrificial curd (*dadhi*) as its substratum nor is it devoid of cognition;

rather, the meaning is that it is established upon the power (*śakti*) of that which is to be expressed. Furthermore, the fifth *cīcāna*, described as the nature of the temple (*prāsādasvarūpa*) with Brahman as its cause, is the designator (*vācaka*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

The meaning is that even the mantra beginning with *vyomavyāpin* is a cause. Now, when it is asked: "In what order are the lords of the causes and the portions of the paths (*adhvabhāga*) presided over by them, [and] by whom are they presided over up to Brahman?"—it is said:
Sadyojāta is indeed proclaimed as the name of Āmā; Viṣṇu is [the deity of] Aghora, while Puruṣa and Īśvara have Rudra as their presiding deity.

Īśvara and Śiva are proclaimed as the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*); the meaning is that the upper portion is presided over by the deity Rudra. Śrava has Śiva as its deity; its upper portion is presided over by Sadāśiva and is governed by Īśāna. These mantras are the presiding deities, and not Brahmā and the others alone.
It should be explained that [these] are the presiding deities of Sadyojāta and the others. This is because it would otherwise contradict the scripture;

for, having established the nature of the *sakala* (the manifest) through the distinction between the signifier and the signified, as well as that which is presided over by them, [the text] now establishes the supreme reality, the nature of Śiva, which is *niṣkala* (unmanifest). As for the mantra, it is the supreme reality to be perceived.
It abides in the qualities.
His body is not to be described as consisting of the material qualities born of *prakṛti*.

However, within the body, there is the sixth [element], beginning with *mā* and situated at the *brahmarandhra*; having gradually attained the transcendence of the body beyond the fivefold [elements] through the abandonment of the causal [state], one reaches the external path (*adhvan*) governed by the five times (*pañcakāla*).

The supreme reality transcends the divisions [of the path] and so forth; its true nature is beyond the conceptualization of words. It is to be known through direct experience alone, and it is characterized by the absence of qualities and measures. One should not imagine that this reality can be burned away by the principles (tattvas) born of primordial matter (prakṛti), produced from the gunas, or arising from the great illusion (mahāmāyā). Rather, it has been stated that it consists solely of its own inherent power (svaśakti).

The supreme nature of reality, because it transcends verbal conceptualization, is beyond inference and is inexpressible; regarding this fruit of knowledge, he said: "Having known the supreme ladder that leads to the fivefold state..."
When knowledge is known by one whose inner self is not struck with wonder, [then he is truly wise].
At that very moment he is liberated, for when that Supreme is known.

Having understood this discourse as a manual for the steps of ascending the throne of Brahman’s empowerment, that which is characterized as "knowledge" is merely an indicative term. Śiva’s own nature consists of both knowledge and action;
when He is known—that is, made an object—by the power of knowledge through a contented inner self, then He alone becomes accessible.

The thought is that it is not improper for the form of another deity to be employed as a residence for the sake of instability; at first... even from that which is supreme with three long syllables (*tryāgurūttama*), Śaṅkara showed favor toward the worlds and bestowed his grace.
From them came the perfection of the established doctrine and the joy of those who move through the celestial realms.

Through the prowess of Mantreśa Rudradeva, prosperity was attained... from the primordial Śivakula arose the lineage of Gurus; its seat is the illustrious place named Āmardaka, and its Gurus are in Bhārata.
By the one who performs various rites arising from that [tradition], has the *golīkaraṇa* (making into a sphere), O Bhadra, been attained among the beloved ones? (p.
86) In the lineage of the Gurus born of that family, by the splendor of Śrīkaṇṭha...
Born in the land of Gommaṭa, he became Śiva through the power of his illustrious meditation. Now, this venerable one attained the status of preceptor to the Lord of Cola;
he who for a long time worshipped the Lord of the Assembly with devotion.

Therefore, there arose from his heart one named Śaṅkara, renowned on the surface of the earth as the sovereign of the Śaivas; he who is the very Śiva in the Vedas, in all the collections of scriptures, and in the Śiva-āgamas, being the life-force of the ritual injunctions.
His disciple was Kāṇḍihya...
born of the lineage of Mābha, a son of Kṛṣṇa who was a treasury of sacred learning; [he was] Bahurūpa Śambhu, whose ocean of speech was filled with the jewels of the *Pātyādi* and other [scriptures].
O Lord, you are the helmsman for those who cross the ocean of scriptural exegesis.

He who composed various pure compositions on the teachings of Śiva with words whose phrases and measures were [perfect], and whom the kings beginning with the Lord of Cola and others, such as Mōhaśūra,
perform worship in places like Śrīmōhaśūra.
Because it is easy to grasp by means of that [method], the Viṃśatikā is proclaimed in the Kālottara.
Thus ends the chapter on the determination of the Prāsāda [mantra] in the commentary on the Dviśatikālottara composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand verses.
The commentary on the Dviśatikālottara is completed.
Peace.
